articles.body:
Marco Rubio: Russia-Ukraine talks 'very productive'

Speaking after Russia, Ukraine and the US held trilateral talks today in the UAE, US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said the talks were “very productive”, but that there was still a lot of work to be done.

Reuters reports Rubio also said that it was a goal at some point to expand the trilateral talks to include other European voices.

Speaking after Russia, Ukraine and the US held trilateral talks today in the UAE, US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said the talks were “very productive”, but that there was still a lot of work to be done. Reuters reports Rubio also said that it was a goal at some point to expand the trilateral talks to include other European voices.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the first day of US-led talks in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine and Russia was “constructive and quite substantive”, after being briefed by Kyiv’s negotiators in UAE. “The trilateral format was constructive and quite substantive,” Zelensky said on X, adding that he “gave our team clear instructions for further dialogue – both in the trilateral format tomorrow and more broadly, over the coming days, with envoys of the US President and representatives of Europe.”

Russia attacked 10 Ukrainian regions overnight, hitting five major energy substations that transmit electricity between regions, Ukrainian prime minister, Sergii Koretskyi, said. The substations that were hit were in the Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad regions, Koretskyi said. Russian attacks killed at least nine people and injured 39 others across Ukraine over the past day, according to a report in the Kyiv Independent.

The European Union will contribute €50m ($55m) to an initiative to improve Black Sea security, EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday, after several attacks on ships in the region. A number of vessels were struck in the Black Sea off Bulgaria and Romania in October, leaving more than 30 sailors dead or missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.

The EU has said it stands ready “to come with a swift and united response” after France blamed Iran for a spate of cyber-attacks on supermarket freezers and chillers that caused millions of euros of damage. Speaking to journalists on Monday, French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible as he announced France believed that Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were “responsible for this attack”.

Iran has responded to the accusation by France that it was responsible for the recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in the European country, declaring them “baseless”. AFP reports that in a statement, Tehran said “Iran’s foreign ministry categorically rejects the French government’s baseless and one-sided accusations against Iran regarding alleged cyber activities in France”, adding that it “strongly condemns this hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against the Islamic republic”.

Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned. In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.

At least 10 people died in a traffic accident involving about 50 vehicles on both sides of a foggy stretch of highway in southeastern Bulgaria this morning, the BTA news agency reported, citing the Yambol regional governor, Georgi Chalakov. Ch Insp Todor Mishinev from the Yambol regional directorate of the ministry of internal affairs told Nova TV that some people were still trapped in their cars.

Hungarian authorities have detained the brother of Viktor Orbán as part of a people-smuggling investigation, the prime minister, Péter Magyar, has said. The Hungarian anti-graft body, the national asset protection and recovery office (NVVH), said in a statement it and police had detained four people and searched homes in Budapest and Pest county.

Portugal will shut schools and non-esesential public services on Wednesday, with Storm Charles expected to bring torrential rain and heavy winds to parts of the country. “All those who can should stay at home,” the country’s interior minister Luis Neves told a press conference on Tuesday, warning people to stay away from coastal areas and to work from home where possible.

A number of vessels were struck in the Black Sea off Bulgaria and Romania in October, leaving more than 30 sailors dead or missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.

During a visit to Bulgaria on Tuesday, von der Leyen said the EU wants to “fast track” the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub and agree “clear timelines for its completion”.

“And we want to offer dedicated funding of 50 million euros” to the initiative, she said.

The hub was proposed in 2025 as a joint Romanian-Bulgarian initiative to boost European presence in the area and counter Russian influence in the wake of Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Von der Leyen also said €10m would be immediately allocated to Bulgarian search and rescue, following a similar announcement in Romania on Monday.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the first day of US-led talks in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine and Russia was “constructive and quite substantive”, after being briefed by Kyiv’s negotiators in UAE.

“The trilateral format was constructive and quite substantive,” Zelensky said on X, adding that he “gave our team clear instructions for further dialogue – both in the trilateral format tomorrow and more broadly, over the coming days, with envoys of the US President and representatives of Europe.”

Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi addressed humanitarian issues, Zelenskyy says

The Reuters news agency has some quotes from Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has been speaking to students during his visit to Denmark.

Asked about the Abu Dhabi trilateral talks, he said that humanitarian issues such as prisoner of war exchanges and bringing back children had been discussed, adding that security guarantees were also on the agenda.

Zelenskyy arrived in Copenhagen earlier today for talks with Nordic leaders on military assistance, air defences and protecting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure from Russian strikes.

Denmark announced a donation of 4.8bn kroner ($720m; £537m) in military aid, but did not disclose which weapons or equipment would be included or when they would be delivered.

Amid relentless Russian attacks, Zelenskyy has been urging allies to accelerate deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles – by far the most effective weapon available to Ukraine for downing Russia’s deadly ballistic missiles.

In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.

Eskelund, who heads the influential Beijing-headquartered body, said European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade, asking themselves: “What is the point of trading?”

As the EU gets tough with China with a deficit running at a record £1bn (€1.18bn) a day and an increasing mood for protectionism in Brussels, Berlin and Paris, he said European countries might need to shift their policies to allow domestic manufacturers to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains, rather than treat them as competitors.

Reuters reports Rubio also said that it was a goal at some point to expand the trilateral talks to include other European voices.

AFP reports that in a statement, Tehran said “Iran’s foreign ministry categorically rejects the French government’s baseless and one-sided accusations against Iran regarding alleged cyber activities in France”, adding that it “strongly condemns this hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against the Islamic republic”.

Talks between Russia, Ukraine and US end after four hours

The first day of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US in the UAE have ended after four hours.

In an update, Bulgaria’s health minister, Katya Ivkova, said 10 people died at the scene and two others died while being transported to hospital, bringing the total deaths to 12. She said 46 other people were transported to medical facilities for treatment.

articles.title: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has first chance to build a new government and oust the prime minister.
articles.preview: Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together. Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
articles.body:
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.

Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.

Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.

Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.

"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.

He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".

Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.

"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.

One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.

The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.

On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government.

Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.

This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".

Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.

The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.

The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue.

The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.

Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside.

If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.

In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.

articles.title: Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
articles.summary: The BBC gains rare access to a specialist drone unit defending the eastern city of Slovyansk from heavy Russian fire.
articles.preview: The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start. "If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs. It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones. But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.
articles.body:
The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start.

"If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.

It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.

But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.

They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.

Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.

Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.

Once inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun â a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.

Abandoned vehicles litter the streets â recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.

Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.

You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.

Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.

Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up â making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.

Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy â to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".

It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas â like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.

Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas â made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.

The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.

October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion â with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.

Before the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.

But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born.

"I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"

Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."

Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.

"It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown".

"I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.

We first met the drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.

Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.

Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.

He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show â "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.

Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day â he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby.

"I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line.

"We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.

The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.

Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far.

"I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".

The next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.

They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.

Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.

"Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."

Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.

Gambia

The race for Gambia's presidency is heating up, as opposition leader Ousainou Darboe officially files his candidacy for the December 5 election.

The 78-year-old leader of the United Democratic Party submitted his nomination papers on Monday, backed by thousands of supporters dressed in the party's signature yellow.

This marks Darboe's sixth attempt at the presidency, after five previous unsuccessful bids.

Once a political ally of incumbent President Adama Barrow, the two fell out in 2019, setting the stage for a renewed political rivalry.

Darboe has described this as his final bid for the presidency, promising to tackle corruption, revive the economy and address the growing youth exodus to Europe.

Meanwhile, the Independent Electoral Commission says it remains on track with the electoral calendar, with candidates expected to learn whether their applications have been approved by November 16.

The ruling National People's Party is also gaining support from other political figures, setting the stage for a competitive presidential contest.

articles.title: Cop31 as it happened: ‘Everything and everyone we love is at stake,’ Greta Thunberg warns
articles.summary: Host Turkey celebrates new oilfields as UN climate summit prepares to host world leaders from more than 90 countries We’ve just heard from Patricia Espinosa , the former UN climate boss (succeeded by Simon Stiell) and now we are hearing from former US secretary of state and climate ambassador, John Kerry. Kerry has congratulated Brazil for keeping the fossil fuel transition issue alive, and the room has erupted in cheers. Continue reading...
articles.preview: Host Turkey celebrates new oilfields as UN climate summit prepares to host world leaders from more than 90 countries We’ve just heard from Patricia Espinosa , the former UN climate boss (succeeded by Simon Stiell) and now we are hearing from former US secretary of state and climate ambassador, John Kerry. Kerry has congratulated Brazil for keeping the fossil fuel transition issue alive, and the room has erupted in cheers. Continue reading...
articles.body:
That’s all for today, thanks for tuning in to our coverage of the second day of the 31st UN climate summit. Here’s a quick recap of the key events:

Scientists said fossil fuel emissions were forecast to flatline for 2026, driven by the Iran war’s shock to oil and gas prices.

Summit host Turkey celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields and its plans to expand fossil fuel production.

The UN secretary-general, António Guterres, called for more work on a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels – an issue that didn’t even make it on to the official agenda.

Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg warned that “everything and everyone we love is at stake”.

We’ll be back tomorrow with more coverage, as the interventions from world leaders begin.

Greenpeace has unveiled a giant limestone boulder carved into the likeness of Sir David Attenborough, which it plans to throw into the North Sea to deter bottom trawling.

Dubbed the “Attenboulder”, the sculpture was revealed aboard the campaign group’s ship Arctic Sunrise on the River Thames on Tuesday.

The unveiling comes as Blue Planet III renews attention on ocean protection.

Will McCallum, Greenpeace UK’s co-executive director, said: “Right off our coasts the government still allows industrial fishing vessels to bulldoze the seabed and all of the incredible marine life it holds.

“These are supposed to be safe havens for wildlife – not killing grounds. The government’s inaction makes a mockery of the term ‘marine protected area’ and is an insult to Attenborough’s urgent work over many years.”

More than 700 groups ranging from trade unions to disability advocates have urged diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.

Building on a commitment at last year’s summit that social movements described as a “historic win”, organisations from 88 countries demanded a mechanism at Cop31 to turn promises of a just transition into action. Known as the Belém-Antalya Mechanism (BAM), it would seek to support issues including human rights, gender equality and good jobs, while respecting Indigenous rights.

“Workers and communities, especially in the Global South, welcomed and celebrated the Cop30 decision to develop a just transition mechanism – or BAM – which has the promise of delivering real support and action for just transition on the ground,” said Lidy Nacpil, coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development. “However, in pre-Cop, governments of the Global North have once again exposed their determination to pour cold water over this promise, by limiting what a mechanism can do and delaying the process of its operationalisation.”

The open letter calls for the mechanism to have the mandate and institutional set-up needed to deliver a just transition – including the ability to provide technical and financial support – as well as giving workers and communities a seat at the table.

'Everything and everyone we love is at stake' - Greta Thunberg

Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, said climate change is “threatening everything” and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”

In comments reported by AP, she told reporters in Antalya: “We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority, and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she told reporters.

Cop31 is the first UN climate summit Thunberg has attended since the Cop26 conference in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021, where she dismissed promises made by global leaders as “blah, blah, blah.”

Since then, fossil fuel emissions have continued to rise – though they flatlined this year – adding even more planet-heating gas to a beleaguered atmosphere. While many big polluters have taken steps to clean up their economies, none are doing so fast enough to keep global heating to the 1.5C Paris climate target.

Here’s a video of Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and president of the Cop31 negotiations, making the case for working together – and the benefits of doing so – at the opening of the summit yesterday. (Subtitles are on.)

Turkey’s celebration of the discovery of two new oilfields last night is already raising eyebrows. While Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s language is more restrained than that of his Azerbaijani counterpart, President Ilham Aliyev, two years ago – when he called oil and gas a “gift from God” at the Cop29 summit – it clashes directly with the strategies to phase out fossil fuels being discussed in Antalya today.

Jeni Miller, head of the Global Climate and Health Alliance, a network of more than 300 health groups addressing climate change, said it sends a “deeply troubling message” to communities where lives, homes and futures are already at stake from climate change and fossil fuel pollution.

“The message from Turkey could not be more contradictory,” said Miller. “How can a country host the world’s most important climate conference – with Cop31 President, Murat Kurum, calling for stronger health systems to protect people from the climate crisis as part of the Antalya Initiative for Resilient Health Systems (AIR) – and on the same day announce plans to expand production of the fossil fuels driving that crisis”

China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.

Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

I’ve been interviewing some of the young climate activists who have gone to the summit. Today I spoke to Yania Hussain Ishan, an 18-year-old climate activist attending Cop31 with the Maldives youth delegation.

She joined a Unicef climate programme at 16 and went on to found Barnacles, a climate initiative working to connect young people.

“Growing up in the Maldives has shaped the way I understand climate change. It’s difficult to separate it from everyday life when so much of what makes our home what it is depends on our environment. I’ve seen how coastlines change, how waves reach roads and public spaces, how flooding affects businesses near the shore, and how rough seas can disrupt the journeys that connect our islands. These are things you grow up seeing, but as you get older, you start thinking a little more about what they mean for the future.

“Sometimes I wonder what the Maldives will look like when I’m older, or what it will be like for children growing up here 20 or 30 years from now. Will they get to experience the same things we did? Will the places we grew up with still feel the same? I don’t think these are questions young people should have to spend so much time worrying about, but for many of us, they’re difficult to ignore.

“At Cop31, I hope we can move beyond repeatedly acknowledging how vulnerable countries like ours are and start paying closer attention to what actually needs to happen. Climate finance, adaptation and loss and damage have very real implications for the lives people get to lead. I also hope young people are given opportunities to meaningfully influence these conversations, rather than simply being invited to participate.

“I think about my own future and what the Maldives will look like by the time I’m older. I want to be able to build my life here, and I want the generations after me to have that same opportunity. I want them to experience the Maldives in all the ways that make it home to us, rather than having to learn about what it once was.”

The death toll from an explosion at a steelworks in western Turkey yesterday has risen to 17 people, Turkish officials have said.

The blast and fire ripped through the iron and steel factory in Aliağa, near Izmir, about 400km northwest of Antalya, on Monday.

In comments reported by AFP, the provincial governor, Suleyman Elban, said a crane fell into a furnace as it was replacing a boiler, which led to an explosion in a nearby steel mill.

The Turkish President, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, offered condolences to the grieving families yesterday, when 16 people were thought to have lost their lives. The death toll has since risen to 17.

'Find the courage to speak the truth to powerful interests' - John Kerry

Graham Readfearn

Now the former US secretary of state, John Kerry, has joined the calls for Cop31 to pick up the mantle of building support to transition away from fossil fuels.

“We are going to have to draw on ourselves and find the courage to speak the truth to powerful interests that seem intent to ignore the basic science.

“We know clean power is cheaper than fossil power. That argument is over except amongst those people who keep wanting to hold on to the past.”

Then the UN secretary general is excused from the stage to attend another meeting, and the room gives him a raucous standing ovation as he walks out.

articles.title: Why is India trying to broker a Russia-Ukraine Black Sea food corridor?
articles.summary: India has influence with both sides, but shipping security and Russia’s cooperation remain major obstacles.
articles.preview: India has influence with both sides, but shipping security and Russia’s cooperation remain major obstacles. India is ready to help broker “food corridors” through the Black Sea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a phone call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday. The announcement came on the eve of United States-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, with Russia and Ukraine returning to the negotiating table after a nine-month pause.
articles.body:
India has influence with both sides, but shipping security and Russia’s cooperation remain major obstacles.

India is ready to help broker “food corridors” through the Black Sea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a phone call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday.

The announcement came on the eve of United States-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, with Russia and Ukraine returning to the negotiating table after a nine-month pause.

Hours later, India’s External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar spoke with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.

Russia and Ukraine have attacked one another’s ports this year, choking off grain and oilseed exports that feed import-dependent countries in Africa and South Asia, and leaving India short of sunflower oil.

What is India offering, why does it want the role, and can it deliver?

What did Zelenskyy and Modi say?

“India is ready to mediate in establishing food corridors, and we are counting on these efforts to continue,” Zelenskyy posted on X after the call. The leaders discussed Russia’s blocking of grain exports in the Black Sea, he said.

Modi did not mention food corridors or the Black Sea, but reaffirmed India’s commitment to contributing “in every possible way” towards a peaceful resolution.

Jaishankar said his call with Lavrov focused on the war and “ongoing diplomatic initiatives”.

What is India offering?

While New Delhi has not published a formal plan, the offer builds on proposals Indian officials floated for weeks.

During a visit to Kyiv in September, Jaishankar reportedly spoke of a potential pause on strikes against Black Sea shipping and energy infrastructure. On October 4, he said India was talking to both Russia and Ukraine about shipping safety, grain and energy exports and “non-attack possibilities”.

“India has become quietly proactive of late,” Praveen Donthi, senior India analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.

Previously, India was “reticent … regarding a mediation role” and limited to “rhetorical calls for diplomacy and dialogue”, he added. Jaishankar’s September visit was a sign of stepping up, he said.

By early October, Kyiv received four ceasefire proposals from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the US.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called India’s proposal “the broadest”, because it covers both the Black Sea and energy infrastructure. The US plan offers only a halt to strikes on energy facilities.

Kyiv says it will accept an energy and Black Sea truce only if the two come together. Russia has so far rejected partial ceasefires, insisting on a comprehensive peace agreement instead.

Ravi Joshi, a visiting fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi and former civil servant, told DD India that “an immediate understanding or a ceasefire is important, and that’s what India can talk about”.

He added that insurance remains a current challenge.

“The ships are not being adequately insured. The insurers are not guaranteeing the safety of the ships,” he said.

Why does India care?

The Black Sea tensions cost India directly.

On November 3, the Ministry of External Affairs said five Indian nationals had been killed in attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and two more had gone missing.

India is also the world’s biggest importer of vegetable oils and buys most of its sunflower oil from Russia and Ukraine. Its edible oil imports fell 7 percent in September.

Sunflower oil imports fell to 108,837 tonnes that month, the lowest since April 2022, the Reuters news agency reported. In October, a 20,000-tonne Russian cargo bound for India was cancelled because of damage to port infrastructure, and about 60,000 tonnes more were delayed.

“For India, this is a priority because this has caused fluctuations in grain prices and increases. So there’s an alignment there,” Maximilian Hess, a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, told Al Jazeera.

According to Donthi, of the International Crisis Group, US President Donald Trump “has accused India of funding the Russian war efforts for buying Russian oil“.

“By mediating in the war, with some concrete proposals, India stands to gain geopolitical heft and credibility that might blunt some of the unwarranted criticism it received in the recent past,” Donthi said, adding: “It will add to its global prestige after having lost some sheen in the past year.”

Why do Black Sea food exports matter?

Before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, about a third of the world’s grain exports passed through the Black Sea, with Ukraine supplying a tenth of global wheat exports and 15 percent of maize, Al Jazeera has reported.

Disruption hits food-importing countries hardest, particularly in Africa and parts of Asia.

This year, the Black Sea has turned into a two-way port war.

Russia has intensified strikes on Ukraine’s Odesa ports, which normally handle about 90 percent of its grain shipments, while Ukraine has hit Russian grain terminals.

In August, Ukraine’s Ministry of Agriculture cut its forecast for 2026-27 agricultural exports by more than half, to about 29.6 million tonnes, RBC-Ukraine reported. By mid-August, attacks on shipping had shut down more than 97 percent of Russia and Ukraine’s grain export capacity in the Azov and Black Sea basin, according to Reuters.

The last deal of this kind, the United Nations- and Turkiye-brokered Black Sea Grain Initiative, allowed nearly 33 million tonnes of food to leave three Ukrainian ports from July 2022, before Russia withdrew a year later.

What makes India a credible broker?

India is one of few major powers with working relationships in both Moscow and Kyiv.

Joshi said India’s strategic autonomy puts it in a position to push for peace because New Delhi is “friends with both” sides.

India has also been even-handed.

In July, it summoned Moscow’s charge d’affaires to condemn a Russian strike on a merchant vessel that killed 10 people, including four Indian crew members. Days later, it summoned Ukraine’s ambassador over an Indian seafarer killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the MV Omorfi, PTI reported.

It is also a customer both sides need.

In the 2025-26 marketing year, India imported 1.46 million tonnes of sunflower oil from Russia and 443,000 tonnes from Ukraine, according to the Indian Solvent Extractors’ Association (SEA), alongside large volumes of Russian crude.

Hess, at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said Zelenskyy approached India “because they have leverage over Moscow, and they are one of the few major buyers of its oil still”.

He added that a large amount of Russian money sits in the Indian financial system, which Moscow wants to keep access to.

What stands in India’s way?

For a start, New Delhi has not publicly confirmed the offer. Modi only spoke of contributing to a peaceful resolution, leaving India’s commitment in question.

Kyiv also has doubts about India’s neutrality. Ukraine has repeatedly pressed New Delhi over its purchases of Russian oil, which Jaishankar defended during his September visit, saying they would not determine the course of the war.

Hess said Zelenskyy “wants to show India that it should perhaps revisit the state of its partnership with Moscow”.

“It’s important for Ukraine to show everybody that Russia isn’t a trustworthy partner,” he said.

India also lacks a physical foothold.

The 2022 grain deal relied on Turkiye, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Bosphorus and hosted the deal’s joint inspection centre in Istanbul. Any new corridor would need ships, insurers and inspections that India cannot supply alone.

The field is crowded, too.

Turkiye, Egypt and the US have all tabled proposals, and the Kremlin says the Abu Dhabi talks are trilateral, with Washington as the sole mediator.

Above all, a corridor would now require both sides to stop. Unlike in 2022, Ukraine is also striking Russian grain terminals. Russia, for its part, walked away from the last grain deal in 2023.

Hess said earlier attempts towards a standalone corridor failed “because Russia kept attacking Ukrainian ports”, and that shipping recovered only when Ukraine used naval drones to push Russia’s fleet away.

What happens next?

Russian and Ukrainian delegations are meeting in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, but talks are stuck on the issue of territory – something that is “impossible to negotiate”, said Joshi.

Hess added, “Russia has yet to offer any concessions and has, in fact, increased its own demands in places. The negotiations and these offers have alternate aims other than an actual deal, but rather to affect the thinking and the positioning of other countries.”

With troop casualty numbers at record highs, Moscow is likely to be facing pressure domestically, he said.

“Russia’s entire purpose of engaging in negotiations with Europe and the United States is to divide and conquer,” Hess said. “For the Russians, [it is] about trying to make the Ukrainians take the blame. For the Ukrainians, it’s about trying to make others see the Russians as acting in bad faith.”

articles.title: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: Tons of chilled and frozen food was spoiled last month as fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heated up.
articles.preview: Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile". On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression". He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.
articles.body:
Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile".

On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression".

He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.

The French cyber-attacks, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food, were followed by a similar hacks against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.

Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".

He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".

France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.

The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.

Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.

Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.

In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.

On Monday, some Iranian media outlets denied the French accusations, but there had been no official comment until Tuesday's statement from Iran's foreign ministry.

On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.

Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.

In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.

The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title: Japan watches for signs of change in Trump's foreign policy priorities
articles.summary: Tokyo fears the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm election may push him to pursue a diplomatic quick win at the expense of Washington's allies in the Indo-Pacific.
articles.preview: November 10, 2026 Tokyo fears the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm election may push him to pursue a diplomatic quick win at the expense of Washington's allies in the Indo-Pacific. With just a week to go before the leaders of the United States, China and Russia are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Japan is closely watching for signs of any shift in Washington's policy toward the Indo-Pacific.
articles.body:
November 10, 2026

Tokyo fears the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm election may push him to pursue a diplomatic quick win at the expense of Washington's allies in the Indo-Pacific.

With just a week to go before the leaders of the United States, China and Russia are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Japan is closely watching for signs of any shift in Washington's policy toward the Indo-Pacific.

The APEC gathering, taking place this year in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, is scheduled for November 18-19.

Tokyo fears that the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm elections may push him to seek a diplomatic quick win, one he can point to as evidence of his statesmanship but that fails to take into account the interests of Washington's allies in the region.

Tokyo has moved swiftly to try to ascertain the mood in a White House that was left reeling by the results of the November 3 midterm election.

Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi held talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris on Monday.

Following their meeting, the Japanese Foreign Ministry released a statement saying that both sides agreed to "further advance security cooperation to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-US alliance."

They also vowed to "maintain close communication" on the situation in the Indo-Pacific, without providing further details.

Why is Japan worried?

"Japan's concern is that with Trump becoming a lame duck in domestic politics, he will use his presidential authorities to shift his focus to foreign policy," said Sebastian Maslow, a professor of politics at the University of Tokyo.

"A US deal with China may provide President Xi [Jinping] the ability to intensify pressure on Japan," he told DW. "With Sino-Japanese relations severely strained, this will put Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi in a difficult position and she will have to reassess how to navigate US-China relations."

Margarita Estévez-Abe, associate professor at Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and an expert on Japanese politics, said Japan fears "a transactional Trump who treats Taiwan as a bargaining chip."

She pointed out that after the May summit with Xi, Trump described US arms sales to Taiwan as "a good negotiating chip with China."

Tokyo is also "frustrated" that Trump has not come to its support over the rare earth export restrictions China imposed on Japan after Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last year, with the Trump administration treating the China-Japan feud as "Tokyo's problem," she said.

Efforts to preserve the geopolitical balance

Furthermore, Japan has concerns about Washington's foreign policy positions toward North Korea and Russia.

"Trump has not damaged the US-Japan alliance the way he has strained NATO, but his outreach to Moscow and Pyongyang worries Tokyo," said Estévez-Abe.

"The US relies on Japan as its main military base in the Indo-Pacific, so it is not in Washington's interest to embolden Russia and North Korea against Japan," she added. "But if American softness does raise the threat to Japan, Japanese trust in the alliance will erode. Japan can only hope that doesn't happen."

Ultimately, Tokyo wants to preserve the geopolitical balance in the region and prevent already strained tensions from escalating further. But Japan is increasingly questioning the commitment of a security and trade partner that has stood by it since 1945.

"Japan's security strategy emphasizes preserving the status quo in terms of defending the liberal international order and containing China's role in the Indo-Pacific," said Maslow. "However, in order to achieve this, Japan has emphasized the role of the US alliance as a cornerstone of its foreign policy and security. The reality still is that Japan has no 'plan B' if the alliance unravels."

Diversifying security partnerships

Efforts to strengthen Japan's military are embedded within the framework of the US-Japan alliance, he pointed out. And while there have been calls for Japan to develop an autonomous defense capability, achieving that in the short term is unrealistic given the limitations of its defense industry and a lack of key resources, including critical intelligence.

Over the past decade, Tokyo has proactively diversified its security partnerships, stepping up defense cooperation with European Union member states and NATO, forging a quasi-alliance with Australia, and joining a range of minilateral frameworks across the Indo-Pacific, including with the Philippines.

This reflects Japan's desire to play a more proactive role in shaping regional and global security, Maslow said.

Tokyo hopes no major clashes erupt in the region for the remaining two years of Trump's term and that Washington's resolve is not tested before a new and "strategically more amenable administration comes in," Estévez-Abe said.

Maslow stressed, however, that "hope is not a strategy" and that Tokyo needs to maintain efforts to protect the alliance and double down by demonstrating its own commitments to security with even greater defense spending and by safeguarding economic security.

articles.title: French judo star Teddy Riner announces run for presidency
articles.summary: Judy star Teddy Rinner wants to be the next president of France. The 37-year-old Olympic champion announced his bid on social media on Monday. The news comes as polls show the French public largely split between the far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melanchon and the far-right's Marine Le Pen.
articles.preview: Judy star Teddy Rinner wants to be the next president of France. The 37-year-old Olympic champion announced his bid on social media on Monday. The news comes as polls show the French public largely split between the far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melanchon and the far-right's Marine Le Pen.
articles.body:
France

Judo star Teddy Riner wants to be the next French president.

The 37-year-old multiple Olympic champion, who is consistently ranked among France’s favorite public figures, announced his bid on social media on Monday. Riner, who has liberal economic views, said in an interview with Le Parisien newspaper that he is positioning himself as “neither right-wing nor left-wing” and hopes to become a “president who brings people together.”

Asked whether his bid should be taken seriously, Riner said “what would be irresponsible would be to remain silent and stand by as a spectator to what is happening in our country, and what has been happening for several years now.”

The French presidential election is being held next year, and campaigning is taking place in a tense social climate.

Protest marches have been drawing huge crowds for weeks in Paris and elsewhere across France as demonstrators demand higher wages and back the country’s student protest movement, piling fresh pressure on the beleaguered government.

Riner said he is aware of the social tensions running through the country and that he can’t accept young people and older generations saying they are struggling to imagine a future for themselves.

“I hear the anger, which some people echo in their rhetoric with a great deal of negativity, coming from people who no longer have any ambition or the desire to think big,” Riner said. “Yet France is a great country. It has allowed me to become the person I am today and given me the opportunity to dream big. Today, that is precisely what is missing. There is no longer that ambition, no longer that hope.”

Riner said in September that he wants to end his stellar career with a fourth individual Olympic gold medal at the Los Angeles Games in 2028. Asked by Le Parisien if his presidential bid means he is giving up on the Olympics, the 2.04-meter heavyweight said no.

“Not if my duties as president allow it and the French people give me their blessing,” the 11-time world champion said.

French authorities in September said they investigated online racial abuse aimed at Riner after he expressed concern about the rise of the far right. In an interview with French sports television show Stade 2, Riner said he was “freaked out” by the rise of extremism. Asked if he meant “on both sides” — meaning the far left and far right — Riner replied “the far right.”

According to opinion polls, the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen is the front-runner to replace Emmanuel Macron, ahead of hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Other aspirants include two former prime ministers of Macron. Candidates from the moderate left and right, the Green party and conservatives, are also running, among others.

“The country is experiencing deep divisions right now, let’s not kid ourselves,” Riner said. “And in the face of that, I don’t see a single candidate putting forward a credible and fair vision capable of bringing the French people together rather than dividing them. There is no one today offering genuine, sincere hope. It’s always one side against another. I’m running for president to show that we can get France back on its feet. We are capable of achieving great things together.”

In order to stand, Riner will need to gather 500 sponsorship signatures from elected officials, as required by French law.

Asked about what would be his first initiative on the international stage if he is elected, Riner said he wants to make sure France works well with its allies and commands greater respect.

“A lot of people around me have been talking about my first handshake with Donald Trump,” he said, laughing. “We’ll see who has the firmer handshake.”

articles.title: L’attentato che ha infranto le certezze della Polonia
articles.summary: La strage di Cracovia ha costretto i polacchi a confrontarsi con una minaccia che credevano lontana. E ha riaperto il dibattito sull’estremismo di destra
articles.preview: “Sei morti e almeno dieci feriti gravi: è il bilancio dell’attentato terroristico di Cracovia, il primo nella storia della Polonia contemporanea. L’autore, un ventiquattrenne di Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, ha sparato con un fucile contro passanti scelti a caso mentre attraversava in auto la piazza del Mercato e le strade della città vecchia. Poco prima aveva ucciso i genitori e la sorella a Ostrowiec. È stato fermato dopo pochi minuti da due agenti di una pattuglia. Nello scontro a fuoco con il terrorista, i poliziotti hanno riportato gravi ferite.
articles.body:
“Sei morti e almeno dieci feriti gravi: è il bilancio dell’attentato terroristico di Cracovia, il primo nella storia della Polonia contemporanea. L’autore, un ventiquattrenne di Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, ha sparato con un fucile contro passanti scelti a caso mentre attraversava in auto la piazza del Mercato e le strade della città vecchia. Poco prima aveva ucciso i genitori e la sorella a Ostrowiec. È stato fermato dopo pochi minuti da due agenti di una pattuglia. Nello scontro a fuoco con il terrorista, i poliziotti hanno riportato gravi ferite.

L’attentatore è stato ferito ed è morto il 9 novembre. Gli inquirenti stanno accertando le motivazioni del suo gesto e stanno cercando di capire se sia stato aiutato da qualcuno”. Così Gazeta Wyborcza racconta l’attentato di Cracovia del 7 novembre, compiuto da Michał Oksiński, un ventiquattrenne affascinato dalle ideologie ultranazionaliste e di estrema destra.

“Guardiamo i filmati di Cracovia. L’eroismo dei poliziotti – che senza esitare si sono lanciati a fermare il terrorista, salvando così la vita a decine di persone – suscita la nostra ammirazione e il nostro più profondo rispetto. Così come la dedizione dei medici e delle altre persone che si trovavano per caso in piazza del Mercato e si sono subito precipitate a soccorrere i feriti”, prosegue il quotidiano polacco. “La portata della tragedia è sconvolgente. Fino a oggi consideravamo la Polonia un paese libero da qualsiasi forma di terrorismo. Chi veniva dall’estero apprezzava il fatto che da noi ci si sentisse al sicuro. Da un decennio vivevamo nella paura di un attacco dall’esterno. Sabato, invece, a uccidere è stato un cittadino polacco”.

“Fino a oggi un attentato simile ci sembrava impensabile. Salivamo su un autobus o entravamo in metropolitana con l’assoluta certezza che, salvo incidenti, saremmo arrivati sani e salvi a destinazione. Un attacco come questo cambierà le nostre vite e la nostra percezione della sicurezza negli spazi pubblici”, scrive il quotidiano di Varsavia Rzeczpospolita. “Le immagini di Cracovia mostrano che la società polacca non ha idea di come comportarsi in situazioni di crisi come queste. Il mondo che conoscevamo appartiene ormai al passato”.

Come spiega il settimanale Polityka, per i polacchi il terrorismo era finora associato all’estremismo islamico (“I terroristi erano combattenti mediorientali con kalashnikov, turbante e infradito, in moto o a bordo di una Toyota Hilux”), e il paese si credeva al riparo dagli attacchi che si verificavano in diverse capitali europee, come Parigi, Berlino, Londra o Bruxelles.

“È così che per i polacchi ha preso forma l’archetipo del terrorista, al quale però l’attentatore di Cracovia, con la sua vecchia Subaru carica di armi, non corrisponde affatto. Eppure questo giovane di Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, nella tranquilla provincia polacca, ha ucciso tre dei suoi familiari più stretti, prima di partire per la sua missione omicida nel centro di Cracovia, affollato di turisti”, scrive Polityka. “A radicalizzarlo non è stato l’islam, ma – secondo i primi accertamenti della polizia – le ideologie di estrema destra. Questa descrizione sommaria non permette di stabilire se l’attentatore perseguisse un progetto preciso. Per il momento non risulta che abbia lasciato messaggi o manifesti”.

“Non facciamoci illusioni: questa tragedia alimenterà – anzi, sta già alimentando – le battaglie politiche combattute nell’ambito della polarizzazione sempre più estrema del nostro paese. L’opposizione la userà contro chi governa, e chi governa contro l’opposizione. E se i rapporti di forza fossero invertiti, se cioè chi oggi governa fosse all’opposizione e viceversa, le cose non cambierebbero”, commenta il settimanale di Cracovia Tygodnik Powszechny.

“Fino a un certo punto è un fenomeno comprensibile”, prosegue il settimanale. “Sono verità in qualche modo banali e già note. Oggi, però, a poche ore dalla tragedia, la cosa più importante è un’altra. Oltre alle vittime e ai loro familiari, vorrei dedicare un pensiero ai due eroici poliziotti che hanno fermato l’assassino. Mettendo a rischio la propria vita, e armati solo di pistole, hanno affrontato un uomo che aveva con sé un intero arsenale. In momenti come questi si capisce con chiarezza cosa siano l’eroismo autentico e il rischio reale, e cosa invece ne sia solo un’imitazione, parole vuote o semplice superbia spacciata per nobiltà d’animo, coraggio e generosità”.

E conclude: “A questi due poliziotti dobbiamo il massimo rispetto e la più profonda gratitudine. Nella vita di tutti i giorni non ci rendiamo neppure conto del ruolo che queste persone svolgono davvero. Del prezzo che pagano per il loro lavoro. Giornate come questa ce lo fanno capire al di là di ogni dubbio. E restituiscono alle cose le giuste proporzioni. O almeno dovrebbero”.

articles.title: Il sindaco di Trieste minaccia chi protesta in sostegno dei migranti
articles.summary: “Se lanciano bombe carta nella mia città, allora io gli sparo in testa”, ha detto Roberto Dipiazza, commentando gli scontri avvenuti durante una manifestazione per dare un riparo a chi dorme in strada
articles.preview: “Se lanciano bombe carta nella mia città, allora io gli sparo in testa”. Le parole sono del sindaco di Trieste Roberto Dipiazza, che l’8 novembre, in un’intervista al quotidiano Il Piccolo, ha commentato gli scontri avvenuti due giorni prima in piazza della Libertà, durante una manifestazione per l’apertura di uno spazio di accoglienza per le persone migranti che dormono in strada. Le dichiarazioni hanno provocato le reazioni delle opposizioni, che hanno chiesto le dimissioni di Dipiazza.
articles.body:
“Se lanciano bombe carta nella mia città, allora io gli sparo in testa”. Le parole sono del sindaco di Trieste Roberto Dipiazza, che l’8 novembre, in un’intervista al quotidiano Il Piccolo, ha commentato gli scontri avvenuti due giorni prima in piazza della Libertà, durante una manifestazione per l’apertura di uno spazio di accoglienza per le persone migranti che dormono in strada. Le dichiarazioni hanno provocato le reazioni delle opposizioni, che hanno chiesto le dimissioni di Dipiazza.

Le proteste a cui si riferiva il sindaco erano state scatenate dalla morte di due persone di 21 e 29 anni in un incendio nel porto vecchio della città. Tra il 1 e il 2 novembre le fiamme erano divampate al Magazzino 18, uno degli edifici abbandonati del porto vecchio. Un uomo e una donna sono morti nel rogo.

Il magazzino è uno dei luoghi in cui da tempo trovano riparo persone migranti e richiedenti asilo arrivati attraverso la rotta balcanica: edifici fatiscenti, senza condizioni minime di sicurezza, diventati l’unica alternativa alla strada per chi non ha un alloggio. Secondo la ricostruzione delle organizzazioni che si occupano di accoglienza, l’incendio sarebbe stato probabilmente causato da un fuoco acceso per scaldarsi.

Non è la prima volta che a Trieste si muore in queste condizioni. In un comunicato, diffuso l’8 novembre dall’assemblea Khandwalarm, si ricordano anche le morti, avvenute lo scorso anno, di Sunil Tamang e Hichem Billal, dovute al freddo e all’indigenza. I magazzini del porto vecchio sono usati da anni come rifugio informale.

Dopo l’incendio, la risposta delle istituzioni, denunciano le associazioni, non è stata aprire uno spazio sicuro, ma sgomberare e chiudere gli edifici. Alcune persone sono state trasferite in altre località italiane, molte altre si sono ritrovate nuovamente in strada.

Il 2 novembre, dopo la morte dei due giovani, circa 250 persone si sono radunate in piazza della Libertà per una commemorazione. C’erano cittadini, volontari, attivisti e migranti. Chiedevano di trovare una soluzione per chi non ha un posto in cui dormire.

Da anni associazioni e organizzazioni si battono per l’apertura dell’ex mercato coperto di via Flavio Gioia, una struttura comunale chiusa dal 2016, a pochi passi dalla stazione e dal porto vecchio. Non si tratta, sostengono i promotori della mobilitazione, di inventare una soluzione da zero.

L’edificio misura 2.330 metri quadrati, ha gli allacciamenti idrici ed elettrici e una ventina tra bagni e docce. Nell’ottobre 2022 comune e prefettura avevano già concordato di trasformarlo in un dormitorio da 90 posti letto, con uno stanziamento di 30mila euro del comune e di 300mila euro del ministero dell’interno. Il progetto era poi saltato dopo un dietrofront della maggioranza in consiglio comunale. Anche i posti nel sistema di accoglienza, secondo i dati riportati dalle associazioni, sarebbero sufficienti.

Il Consorzio italiano di solidarietà - Ics, che gestisce l’accoglienza diffusa in città, avrebbe da mesi circa settanta posti liberi nei propri appartamenti, mentre un centinaio di persone continua a dormire per strada o nei magazzini del porto vecchio. Ma il ministero dell’interno non assegna i posti alle persone che hanno fatto la domanda di asilo. Molti richiedenti, inoltre, restano esclusi dall’accoglienza perché la questura ritarda la formalizzazione delle domande, assegnando appuntamenti a distanza di settimane o mesi.

È quanto documenta il rapporto Accesso negato, pubblicato nel dicembre 2025 da Ics, Diaconia valdese, Linea d’ombra e altre organizzazioni. Un’attesa durante la quale le persone restano senza alloggio e senza accesso all’assistenza sanitaria ordinaria, nonostante il diritto all’accoglienza, ricordano le associazioni, sorga dal momento in cui viene manifestata la volontà di chiedere asilo.

C’è poi un altro aspetto: dal 14 ottobre la questura ha vietato la distribuzione di pasti, vestiti e coperte in piazza della Libertà il sabato e la domenica, limitandola negli altri giorni alla fascia oraria tra le 18 e le 20. Tra le motivazioni indicate ci sarebbe la necessità di garantire lo svolgimento delle attività di intrattenimento della città. Una decisione che, secondo le organizzazioni, finisce per rendere invisibili le persone che vivono in strada e chi cerca di assisterle.

È in questo contesto che il 6 novembre circa duecento persone si sono ritrovate in piazza della Libertà. L’assemblea era nata spontaneamente dalla volontà di chi aveva partecipato alla commemorazione dei due ragazzi morti nell’incendio. Il gruppo aveva deciso di raggiungere l’ex mercato di via Flavio Gioia e aprirlo, perché dare riparo a chi dorme all’aperto. Secondo il comunicato delle organizzazioni, i partecipanti sono entrati gradualmente nei locali, dove hanno trovato ambienti riscaldati, bagni e docce in buone condizioni.

Hanno chiesto di trattare con le autorità, ma sono arrivati due reparti antisommossa di polizia e carabinieri che hanno respinto i manifestanti con scudi e manganelli.La ricostruzione dei partecipanti è diversa da quella circolata nelle prime ore dopo gli incidenti. Dopo una prima fase di cariche, una persona ha lanciato un petardo. I manifestanti sostengono che non si sia trattato di una bomba carta, come riportato da alcune cronache. Le forze dell’ordine hanno ripreso le cariche con maggiore intensità.

Nel comunicato si parla di quattro persone con trauma cranico, una ragazza con tre giorni di prognosi, una persona con due dita fratturate mentre cercava di proteggere una manifestante caduta a terra e una dozzina di persone con lividi. Una persona è stata fermata e portata in questura, per essere rilasciata circa un’ora dopo.

Tra i presenti c’era anche la consigliera regionale Giulia Massolino, che ha raccontato di aver assistito all’assemblea e all’azione davanti all’ex mercato: “I manifestanti erano pacifici. Sono arrivate due squadre di poliziotti in tenuta antisommossa. I manifestanti chiedevano di parlare con il prefetto e il questore. La risposta sono stati i manganelli”.

Massolino ha confermato il lancio di un petardo, ma ha contestato la presenza di una bomba carta e ha definito l’apertura dell’edificio un atto di disobbedienza civile. Il giorno dopo sono arrivate le dichiarazioni del sindaco Dipiazza.

Il 9 novembre le organizzazioni solidali hanno convocato un nuovo presidio in piazza Unità d’Italia, in concomitanza con il consiglio comunale a cui hanno partecipato un centinaio di persone. Hanno chiesto l’apertura immediata dell’ex mercato di via Gioia e una gestione delle richieste d’asilo che non lasci le persone per mesi senza un tetto. La domanda che attraversa la mobilitazione è semplice: se gli spazi esistono, se ci sono posti disponibili e se una soluzione era già stata individuata quattro anni fa, perché a Trieste si continua a morire nei magazzini del porto? ◆
