articles.title: Indonesia VP Gibran expresses intent to step down, presidential official says
articles.summary: Presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi denied reports that President Prabowo Subianto rejected Gibran Rakabuming Raka's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it.
articles.preview: Presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi denied reports that President Prabowo Subianto rejected Gibran Rakabuming Raka's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it. JAKARTA: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka expressed his intention to step down during a meeting on Tuesday (Nov 10) with President Prabowo Subianto, a senior official said, as lawmakers weigh the possibility of a probe into Gibran's eligibility.
articles.body:
Presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi denied reports that President Prabowo Subianto rejected Gibran Rakabuming Raka's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka expressed his intention to step down during a meeting on Tuesday (Nov 10) with President Prabowo Subianto, a senior official said, as lawmakers weigh the possibility of a probe into Gibran's eligibility.

"During the discussion, the vice-president expressed his intention to resign in light of the evolving situation," presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi told reporters.

Prasetyo denied reports that Prabowo rejected Gibran's request, but stopped short of saying the president had accepted it.

At a press conference on Tuesday, Gibran said that Prabowo had advised him to legally contest recent court rulings that found that he was ineligible for office, after he had expressed his intention to resign.

"I respect all the aspirations, criticisms, and suggestions from the public regarding the current situation. I do not want these developments to turn into a prolonged political controversy.

"(Prabowo) offered a great deal of advice and input concerning the current situation. One of his suggestions was that I should continue to pursue my case at the Administrative Court by presenting all my academic records ...," said Gibran.

The meeting came amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Gibran's influential father, the popular two-term former President Joko Widodo, better known as Jokowi.

Gibran helped Prabowo win the 2024 election by a huge margin, but some lawmakers are seeking to investigate whether incomplete education documents he submitted as a candidate disqualify him as vice president.

Gibran, 39, had kept a low profile as vice-president, and his appearances together with Prabowo have been infrequent in their first two years in office.

But he has been thrust into the spotlight of late as tensions grow between the president and Jokowi, who twice defeated Prabowo in 2014 and 2019 elections before tacitly backing him as his successor.

Lawmakers in parliament, which is overwhelmingly under the control of Prabowo's "big tent" coalition, have been looking into launching an inquiry, which some analysts believe could be the first step towards Gibran's impeachment.

The dispute over Gibran's qualifications came after rulings last month by the Constitutional Court and Supreme Court that the education documents he submitted did not meet election requirements.

The constitutional court, however, said it did not have the power to disqualify him, which was the responsibility of other institutions.

On Monday, three senior politicians from the Indonesian Solidarity Party (PSI) serving in Prabowo's Cabinet collectively announced their resignations from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep. Kaesang is Gibran's younger brother and the party had supported the latter in the 2024 presidential election.

The resignations come amid PSI's efforts to strengthen support ahead of the 2029 elections. Since its founding in 2014, PSI has failed to win seats in the House of Representatives in the two elections it has contested - in 2019 and 2024.

articles.title: Are Japan and the U.S. losing South Korea as an ally?
articles.summary: Washington's trust in the South Korean government on intelligence matters seems increasingly fragile.
articles.preview: The poor showing by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections has weakened his administration politically, raising questions about the future of American foreign policy and Washington’s commitment to longstanding alliances. These uncertainties are particularly consequential in Northeast Asia, where strains in the U.S.-South Korea alliance threaten trilateral security cooperation with Japan.
articles.body:
The poor showing by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections has weakened his administration politically, raising questions about the future of American foreign policy and Washington’s commitment to longstanding alliances.

These uncertainties are particularly consequential in Northeast Asia, where strains in the U.S.-South Korea alliance threaten trilateral security cooperation with Japan.

Since South Korean President Lee Jae Myung took office after a snap election in June 2025, tensions in the alliance have grown, jeopardizing cooperation among Washington, Tokyo and Seoul as regional threats mount. Latent friction in the alliance stems from a steady accumulation of Seoul’s subtle pro-Beijing signals, perhaps due to its growing deference to Beijing’s preferences on intelligence and regional deterrence.

articles.title: U.S. allies need a plan for a lame-duck Trump
articles.summary: Some countries, including Iran and Israel, are concerned about how Trump will react to his defeat.
articles.preview: Conventional wisdom has it that after U.S. President Donald Trump suffered a stinging rebuke from American voters this month, losing both houses of Congress, he’s now all the more likely to lash out via foreign policy — the one area where his power remains undiluted. That has Ukrainians fretting (and Russia’s state-controlled media speculating) that Trump could blame them for his defeat, decide that his legacy depends on forcing their capitulation to Moscow or both. Iranians worry he could try to “finish” them.
articles.body:
Conventional wisdom has it that after U.S. President Donald Trump suffered a stinging rebuke from American voters this month, losing both houses of Congress, he’s now all the more likely to lash out via foreign policy — the one area where his power remains undiluted.

That has Ukrainians fretting (and Russia’s state-controlled media speculating) that Trump could blame them for his defeat, decide that his legacy depends on forcing their capitulation to Moscow or both. Iranians worry he could try to “finish” them. Israelis are concerned he may follow the shifting tide of opinion against them. And if Cuba’s leaders didn’t already assume they’re on his menu, they now should.

Some of those fears may well materialize, but it’s far from clear how the least predictable U.S. president in memory will react. The one sure bet — as my Bloomberg Opinion colleague and Trump biographer Timothy O’Brien put it Thursday — is to expect volatility. Trump, he writes, has always tended “to double down when he fails, with little regard for consequences.”

articles.body:
US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine as trilateral talks got under way in Abu Dhabi, the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.

The talks, which are set to go into a planned second day on Wednesday, are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who like Vladimir Putin was not in Abu Dhabi, described the discussions on the first day as “constructive and fairly substantive”.

“We discussed in detail the substance of security guarantees for Ukraine and the foundations for their long-term implementation,” he said in a social media post.

Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

European officials held separate discussions on Tuesday with representatives from Ukraine and the US, where they agreed “any future arrangements must respect sovereignty, territorial integrity, independent decision-making, and provide credible security guarantees for Ukraine”, according to a joint statement.

European leaders are not convinced Russia intends to negotiate in good faith and want to be involved in discussions, although there are signs of unease about the proliferating strands of peace talks. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, last week complained about the “disorderly” process of meetings and phone calls that, she argued, weakened Europe’s ability to speak with one voice.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Tuesday it was a goal at some point to expand the Russia-US-Ukraine talks to include other European voices.

“There’s always this concern in Europe that they’re going to be left out, that America’s going to cut some deal with Russia and leave Europe out of the equation. Well, Europe’s at the table. They’re with us,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Paris, speaking after the UAE talks had finished for the day.

Since his first decade in power, Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protects member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.

“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed scepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the US, described a potential new framework for Europe in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.

A European security official said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

The EU high representative for foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, told a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday: “We already have a European security architecture in place. This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”

Trump has also said that Ukraine would probably be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape”.

After meeting the Kremlin adviser Kirill Dmitriev last week, Trump said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

At that time, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal, and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

The US administration official said: “We have to build something new that works today … Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war.”

articles.summary: Nuovo round di colloqui oggi e domani sulla guerra in Ucraina ad Abu Dhabi. 'Usa mai contrari a colloqui diretti Europa-Russia'. Zelensky: 'colloqui costruttivi'
articles.preview: Al via da oggi e fino a domani ad Abu Dhabi un nuovo round di negoziati sulla guerra in Ucraina, con un formato trilaterale Russia-Ucraina-Stati Uniti, mediato da Washington. articles.body:
Al via da oggi e fino a domani ad Abu Dhabi un nuovo round di negoziati sulla guerra in Ucraina, con un formato trilaterale Russia-Ucraina-Stati Uniti, mediato da Washington.

"Come sapete, la Russia sta partecipando ai colloqui ad Abu Dhabi. Anche l'Ue è presente e, come è stato sottolineato anche in una dichiarazione rilasciata questa mattina, l'obiettivo è quello di arrivare a discussioni in un formato multilaterale: non possiamo dire in questo preciso momento quando ciò avverrà ma questo sarà, in definitiva, l'obiettivo". Lo ha detto la portavoce della Commissione Europea.

"La strada da fare è ancora lunga. Comunque, è un bene che stiano dialogando, è positivo che i colloqui trilaterali siano ripresi. E' sempre meglio che non avere alcun dialogo": lo afferma il segretario di Stato Usa Marco Rubio sui colloqui trilaterali in corso ad Abu Dhabi. Gli Stati Uniti "non si sono mai opposti" a colloqui diretti tra Europa e Russia, "erano i russi a non volerlo", ha aggiunto.

Gli Stati Uniti vogliono un nuovo quadro di sicurezza per l'Ucraina, la Russia e l'Europa al fine di garantire la pace: lo ha affermato ad Abu Dhabi l'inviato statunitense Jared Kushner, in occasione dell'avvio dei colloqui tra i paesi in conflitto. "La speranza oggi non è solo quella di discutere delle questioni bilaterali tra i paesi e di come porre fine alla guerra, ma anche di come creare le giuste relazioni di sicurezza tra Ucraina, Russia ed Europa, in modo da non solo porre fine a questa guerra, ma anche creare un nuovo quadro" per garantire "decenni, se non secoli, di pace", ha affermato Kushner.

Vladimir Medinsky, capo della delegazione russa ad Abu Dhabi e consigliere presidenziale, ha espresso la speranza che i colloqui trilaterali con Usa e Ucraina consentano di "compiere progressi verso la pace". "Ci auguriamo che l'incontro odierno, con la sua composizione rappresentativa, la nostra delegazione ora più ampia e ancora più professionale, ci permetta di avanzare verso la pace nell'interesse dei popoli di Russia e Ucraina", ha dichiarato in apertura dei colloqui Medinsky, citato da Tass.

Zelensky,: 'I colloqui ad Abu Dhabi costruttivi, parlato di garanzie di sicurezza'

I colloqui trilaterali tenutisi oggi ad Abu Dhabi sulla guerra in Ucraina sono stati "costruttivi e approfonditi", e "si è parlato in dettaglio dei contenuti delle garanzie di sicurezza per l'Ucraina" e su come "assicurare che tali garanzie funzionino nel lungo periodo": lo afferma su X il leader di Kiev, Volodymyr Zelensky, riferendo di un resoconto ricevuto dai negoziatori. "Si è discusso della necessità e dei possibili parametri delle misure umanitarie. La liberazione dei prigionieri è una priorità", ha aggiunto Zelensky, che ha dato istruzioni "per proseguire il dialogo" nei colloqui previsti domani e "nei prossimi giorni".

Palazzo Chigi: 'L'accordo per Kiev passa da scelte europee, serve una voce unica'

Il negoziato sull'Ucraina tocca "sempre più da vicino la sicurezza dell'intero continente. Molti elementi di un accordo complessivo dipendono da decisioni europee: garanzie di sicurezza, ricostruzione, sanzioni e percorso europeo dell'Ucraina. Per questo l'Europa deve parlare con una voce sola e dotarsi di un mandato chiaro e condiviso". Così fonti di Palazzo Chigi dopo l'avvio dei colloqui ad Abu Dhabi. Si tratta, spiegano le stesse fonti, di quanto la presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni ha chiesto nella lettera indirizzata al presidente Antonio Costa: discutere il tema in occasione del Consiglio europeo informale di Dublino, per arrivare a una decisione al Consiglio europeo di dicembre. Palazzo Chigi accoglie con favore la disponibilità di Costa a dare seguito alla richiesta e a portare avanti la questione.

Europa-Usa: 'Garanzie di sicurezza credibili a Kiev cruciali per accordo'

"I partecipanti hanno sottolineato che qualsiasi accordo futuro dovrà rispettare la sovranità, l'integrità territoriale e l'autonomia decisionale dell'Ucraina, oltre a fornire garanzie di sicurezza credibili a favore del Paese". Lo afferma una dichiarazione comune dopo l'incontro odierno ad Abu Dhabi tra l'Ue, la Francia, la Germania, l'Italia, il Regno Unito, l'Ucraina, gli Stati Uniti e la Nato. Nella nota si afferma "chiaramente che una Nato forte rimarrà fondamentale per la difesa collettiva euro-atlantica".

articles.summary: Israel has killed more than 1,600 people in Gaza since last year's 'ceasefire', the enclave's Health Ministry says.
articles.preview: Israel has killed more than 1,600 people in Gaza since last year’s ‘ceasefire’, the enclave’s Health Ministry says. Israeli forces have killed at least six Palestinians, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in the Gaza Strip, according to local health sources. Three people were killed on Tuesday in an Israeli air attack on the Ghubain family home in Gaza City’s Daraj area. A father and son were killed in a separate air attack on a tent in the city’s Zeitoun neighbourhood, and a man was killed by Israeli gunfire in the southern city of Khan Younis.
articles.body:
Israel has killed more than 1,600 people in Gaza since last year’s ‘ceasefire’, the enclave’s Health Ministry says.

Israeli forces have killed at least six Palestinians, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in the Gaza Strip, according to local health sources.

Three people were killed on Tuesday in an Israeli air attack on the Ghubain family home in Gaza City’s Daraj area. A father and son were killed in a separate air attack on a tent in the city’s Zeitoun neighbourhood, and a man was killed by Israeli gunfire in the southern city of Khan Younis.

Gaza continues to face regular Israeli attacks despite last year’s “ceasefire”. In fact, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed by Israel in the besieged enclave since the United States-brokered truce agreement, according to the territory’s Ministry of Health.

More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since October 7, 2023, the ministry said.

The killings come as the first strong storm of the season over the weekend flooded about 70,000 tents in Gaza within 12 hours, killing at least five people and causing about $3m in damage, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

Israel is blocking 60,000 mobile homes and 200,000 tents, allowing only 20,000 tents into Gaza, where about 85 percent of homes have been destroyed or damaged by the war. It is also restricting much-needed humanitarian aid.

Negotiators, meanwhile, have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops from Gaza, which controls about two-thirds of the territory and from which Palestinian residents have been ordered to leave.

articles.body:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

articles.title: ‘Positive momentum’: Is the US war on Iran about to end?
articles.summary: Domestic pressures are injecting new life into stalled diplomatic talks, but analysts say peace still hangs by a thread.
articles.preview: Domestic pressures are injecting new life into stalled diplomatic talks between Washington and Tehran, but analysts say peace still hangs by a thread. Diplomatic efforts to end the United States-Israel war on Iran have gathered pace, potentially reducing the chance of another round of intense conflict. US President Donald Trump and Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani hailed positive closed-door talks at the White House on Monday, with Trump saying he considers the war “effectively” at an end.
articles.body:
Domestic pressures are injecting new life into stalled diplomatic talks between Washington and Tehran, but analysts say peace still hangs by a thread.

Diplomatic efforts to end the United States-Israel war on Iran have gathered pace, potentially reducing the chance of another round of intense conflict.

US President Donald Trump and Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani hailed positive closed-door talks at the White House on Monday, with Trump saying he considers the war “effectively” at an end.

But amid talk of peace, both sides have boasted that their militaries are ready and Iran has come under attack.

The US “is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made”, Trump said, but added there would likely be no reason to use it as negotiations with Tehran are “going very well”.

Iran pointed to the possibility of a diplomatic solution while maintaining a deterrence posture.

On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the war would “not end either through military means or by increasing sanctions”, but only through “using the language of respect”.

The comment came a day after Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had hinted at an openness to negotiations, telling the country’s leadership to end the “no war, no peace” reality.

“We can hold talks with dignity and bring the matter to an end with dignity,” Pezeshkian said.

US domestic pressures driving peace

The crushing Republican defeat in the US midterm elections earlier this month is one of the elements injecting new life into stalled diplomatic talks between Washington and Tehran, analysts say.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance both acknowledged that the conflict – which rattled the global energy market and contributed to the rising cost of living – played a significant role in the Democratic Party taking firm control of Congress.

Negar Mortazavi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy in Washington, DC, said the Republican losses “dramatically raised the political cost of more escalation”.

“The Democratic blue tsunami, powered by progressive and antiwar candidates, pushed the party overnight toward a stronger and more united opposition to war,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera.

US House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the next speaker of the House of Representatives in January, told reporters on Monday that the Democratic Party will “end the war in Iran one way or the other”.

Outgoing Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie moved to impeach US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress just days after the midterm elections.

Mortazavi said the result gives the Democrats a stronger mandate to challenge the unpopular war.

“If Democrats unite and use their new power aggressively, they can make it increasingly difficult for Trump to continue the war, pressuring him to end it,” he added.

‘Political and strategic costs of escalation keep growing’

Additionally, Trump’s main ally in the war, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, faces an uncertain political future after the October 27 general election.

His rival Gadi Eisenkot was tasked on Saturday with forming a new government coalition that can survive the opposition of the right-wing bloc led by Netanyahu.

Mortazavi said a third element was Qatar’s intensive mediation, including high-level engagement with both Washington and Tehran, which is creating a diplomatic pathway out of the conflict.

Oil prices fell sharply on Monday amid renewed hopes for diplomatic talks, easing inflation concerns. A diplomatic breakthrough could result in a sustained reduction in energy costs and consumer prices.

“A diplomatic breakthrough is not guaranteed, but the political and strategic costs of escalation keep growing, making another round of war less likely,” Mortazavi said. “Ultimately, Trump will have to decide whether to accept a negotiated end to the war or prolong a conflict with diminishing political support.”

Iran braces for escalation as ‘breakthrough’ appears elusive

Iranian leaders have long maintained that actions speak louder than words when it comes to Washington.

US attacks against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz and on the island of Qeshm have been a daily occurrence. Tehran has reacted by downing US aircraft and controlling marine traffic on the key waterway.

Meanwhile, the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier strike group and the US 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit and its Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group are expected to reach the Middle East later this month.

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei on Monday accused Washington of spreading “fake news” about potential negotiations, demanding that the US accept Tehran’s seven conditions, including the removal of the naval blockade and the unfreezing of Iranian assets.

Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said accepting this “would come at a huge cost” for the Trump administration.

“Reaching a diplomatic arrangement without securing any nuclear concessions from Iran would amount to an admission of defeat, and the Americans seem reluctant to accept that,” he told Al Jazeera. “What regional countries, particularly Qatar, have been trying hard to do is bridge this gap. There is still no sign of a breakthrough on these issues.”

To break the impasse, Azizi said Trump might “launch a major but largely symbolic attack against Iran’s nuclear facilities in order to claim victory and end the war,” even if Iranians are prepared to escalate in response.

In a phone interview with C-SPAN’s Washington Journal Primetime on Monday, Trump said, “We may have to hit Pickaxe Mountain”, which the US says hosts an Iranian nuclear site being constructed deep underground.

On Saturday, Trump called US attacks against Iran’s Qeshm island, in the Strait of Hormuz, “minor strikes” targeting Iranian air defences and launchers.

Another scenario could see the US naval blockade on Iranian ports continue, in the hope of getting more concessions from Tehran.

On his Truth Social platform, Trump claimed on Monday that Gulf countries favour maintaining the blockade of Iran’s economy rather than escalating the war, which would be “approximately five times bigger than the first hit”.

Azizi argued that while this may seem like a lower-cost option for the US and its Gulf allies, it is inherently unsustainable because Tehran has made it clear – most recently with the Supreme Leader’s statement – that it sees the blockade as a continuation of the war.

“It would only be a matter of time before the Iranians decide to escalate significantly against the US naval forces involved in the blockade. It is still unclear to what extent they have the technical capability to hit US warships, but given how rapidly Iran’s missile program has been developing, one should not rule out that possibility,” the analyst said.

“And if that happens, we may end up in the same large-scale war scenario that everyone, including the US, has been trying to avoid.”

articles.body:
Argentina has told an international tribunal that Britain’s approval of oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has dramatically deepened a sovereignty dispute that led to war four decades ago.

At the start of an historic legal clash at the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos), an Argentinian legal team argued that the oil project must be suspended.

Javier Oyarzábal, chief legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said that the 3,400 inhabitants of the Falkland Islands, whose status as a British overseas territory is disputed by Buenos Aires, had no right to the resources around the south Atlantic archipelago.

Oyarzábal said: “[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution … What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong …

“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands whose interests will be duly taken into account.”

Oyarzábal said Argentina was ready to negotiate “all aspects of the question” of the Falkland Islands, which are known as the Malvinas in Argentina, “including the present aggravation of the dispute caused by the UK”.

He accused the UK of refusing to enter talks over the islands while pushing forward on the exploitation of its natural resources in a way that would entrench the status quo.

Oyarzábal claimed that the oil money from the drilling would “finance the very military base and presence that sustains the UK’s de facto control of the territory”.

Addressing the panel’s chair, Judge Maurice Kamga, from Cameroon, he added: “Mr President, the UK cannot have it both ways. It cannot invoke the sovereignty dispute to escape jurisdiction [of Itlos] while exploiting the natural resources of the disputed area as if a dispute had already been resolved in its favour.”

The Sea Lion project in the North Falkland basin, led by the Israeli-firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper, has the potential to triple the islands’ GDP per capita.

It has been condemned as unlawful by Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and his government has applied for arbitration by Itlos over the future of the project, claiming Britain’s approval of is in breach of a 1976 UN resolution calling on both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands until the sovereignty dispute is settled.

Argentina is requesting urgent provisional measures, including a commitment from the UK to “stop the drilling” which, Oyarzábal said would do no more than “preserve the present situation” and allow for constructive talks over sovereignty to begin.

At the start of the two-day hearing, the tribunal’s panel was told that a decision by the UK government to allow drilling to start in March next year was the “unilateral conduct” of a “colonial power”.

It was further claimed by Argentina that the Sea Lion oil project risked an environmental disaster on Argentina’s doorstep and that it would make the sovereignty dispute over the islands “more difficult or impossible” to resolve peacefully.

He added: “In the event of a blowout or spill, it is Argentina that would bear its consequences and be called upon to respond, not a state that is 12,700km away. More over the project lies within the search and rescue region for which Argentina is responsible”.

The long-standing dispute between Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the Falklands led to war in 1982 at the cost of the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.

The hearing is the first time that substantive matters relating to the Falklands have been litigated at an international tribunal.

The oil project is seen on the islands as offering the opportunity to secure their economic future, and build a sovereign wealth fund, at a time when fisheries catches on which they depend are declining.

In a show of solidarity, Princess Anne arrived in Port Stanley on Monday. Ellie Reeves, the UK’s attorney general, attended the Itlos hearing on Tuesday.

She claimed that Argentina was seeking to litigate the issue of sovereignty through Itlos, an independent judicial body established by the 1982 United Nations convention on the law of the sea to oversee maritime disputes.

She said: “We don’t think this is the forum to effectively determine sovereignty issues.”

Asked whether the UK would abide by any ruling, Reeves said: “We don’t know what’s going to happen in terms of the outcome but we don’t consider they have jurisdiction on sovereignty issues. We respect the court and the institutions … but I don’t want to get ahead of what the tribunal may or may not say.” The hearing continues.

articles.title: Hegseth impeachment: What is he accused of, and could he be removed?
articles.summary: Eight articles brought by a Republican lawmaker accuse US Pentagon chief of waging unlawful wars on Iran and Venezuela.
articles.preview: Eight articles brought by a Republican lawmaker accuse the US Pentagon chief of waging unlawful wars on Iran and Venezuela. US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is facing possible impeachment after Republican Congressman Thomas Massie introduced a resolution to remove him from office. articles.body:
Eight articles brought by a Republican lawmaker accuse the US Pentagon chief of waging unlawful wars on Iran and Venezuela.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is facing possible impeachment after Republican Congressman Thomas Massie introduced a resolution to remove him from office.

On Monday, Massie took the floor of the House of Representatives to accuse Hegseth of carrying out unlawful orders and contravening the United States Constitution by waging war against Iran and Venezuela, as well as systematically failing to protect civilians.

He introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday, starting a two-day countdown that could bring a vote by midweek.

Top Democrats say they will support the resolution, while Hegseth has struck a defiant tone and has the backing of US President Donald Trump.

Here’s what we know.

How does impeachment work?

The US Constitution gives the House of Representatives “the sole Power of Impeachment”, meaning it alone can choose to initiate impeachment proceedings against senior officials, including cabinet members.

Officials can be impeached and removed for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors”.

If a majority of the House votes to impeach a cabinet member, the Senate then gets to decide by majority whether to acquit or to convict and remove them. Conviction requires a two-thirds majority of Senate votes.

President Trump made history during his first term in office by becoming the only US president to be impeached by a Democrat-held House twice, though he was acquitted by a Republican-held Senate twice.

If impeached, Hegseth would be the second head of the US military to meet that fate since William Belknap, who was impeached for bribery in 1876.

In this case, Hegseth stands accused of “high crimes and misdemeanors” over his handling of the war on Iran and the conflict with Venezuela.

What is Hegseth accused of?

Of the eight articles, four concern Iran and two cover Venezuela and strikes on boats conducted in the Caribbean since 2025. One relates to the 2025 US air campaign in Yemen. The only non-conflict-related article is Hegseth’s treatment of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly.

Kelly, an Arizona Democrat and retired US Navy captain, appeared with five other Democratic lawmakers in a November 2025 video telling US troops: “Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders.”

Hegseth accused them of sedition and threatened to prosecute them, while Trump said in a social media post that their conduct was “punishable by DEATH!”

Massie’s articles accuse Hegseth of trying to subject the speech and oversight activities of members of Congress “to the will and discretion” of the Department of Defense.

What do the articles say about Iran, Venezuela and Yemen?

Massie said that while Trump was culpable for issuing what he described as unlawful orders, like attacking Iran, Hegseth chose to carry them out.

“Hegseth should not carry out illegal orders, and that’s why we’re impeaching him,” Massie said.

Three of the four Iran articles rest on the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 law that limits a president’s power to wage war without the approval of Congress.

The Iran articles accuse Hegseth of:

- Going to war without the approval of Congress or an attack on the US.

- Ignoring a resolution passed by both chambers of Congress in June that ordered US forces out of the fighting.

- Continuing the war after a 60-day limit for unauthorised hostilities ran out on May 1.

- Taking measures to “systematically dismantle civilian-protection infrastructure”, and responsibility for the Minab school strike that killed 156 civilians, mostly children, on the first day of the war.

The articles accuse Hegseth of fostering a culture “hostile to the law of armed conflict and the protection of civilians”. They cite his declaration in September 2025, as he rebranded the Department of Defense as the Department of War: “Maximum lethality, not tepid legality. Violent effect, not politically correct.”

At a media briefing on Monday, Massie dismissed a claim that the Minab school strike was a mistake caused by the fog of war, saying the US had months to prepare its unilateral attack on Iran.

“There’s no fog of war on the first day,” he said.

In January, US special forces abducted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in a raid on Caracas, after months of US strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.

The articles accuse Hegseth of:

- Committing an act of war against Venezuela without the approval of Congress by abducting Maduro.

- Using drug enforcement as cover for a bid to control Venezuela’s oil.

- Carrying out the extrajudicial killings of at least 243 people in at least 69 boat strikes since September 2025, mostly in international waters.

- Denying quarter to shipwrecked targets who posed no threat and striking them again.

Massie dismissed the administration’s description of the raid on Maduro as a law enforcement operation.

“It was to kidnap a foreign leader so we could take their oil,” he said.

Regarding the US bombing campaign against Yemen’s Houthi group in 2025, Hegseth is accused of:

- Launching the campaign without a declaration of war, approval from Congress, or an attack on the US, in breach of the War Powers Resolution.

- Pressing ahead even though Trump did not notify Congress until 13 days after the strikes began.

- Directing an operation that killed an estimated 224 civilians.

- Ordering the strikes knowing there was no imminent threat.

The article cites a leaked Signal chat between Hegseth and other senior Trump administration officials involved in the planning and execution of the Yemen attack.

Massie said everyone in the chat agreed there was no imminent threat that would justify bypassing Congress. “The consequence of that was civilians killed,” he said.

How has Hegseth responded?

Hegseth held a press conference on Tuesday where he struck a defiant tone.

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt,” he said, referring to the impeachment motion. “And everybody knows it.”

Arguing that the conflicts he oversaw were “lawful military operations”, he castigated Massie for trying to impeach him for what he called “policy disagreements”.

“The proper remedy for a policy disagreement is legislation,” he said. “It’s debate. It’s the next presidential election. It’s not handing the House and Senate floor to Democrats so they can run a show trial against the president and Secretary of War.”

He defended his track record and the US campaigns in Iran and Latin America while warning that punishing him would be the first step in prosecuting soldiers for “doing their job”.

“If they want to come after the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me,” he said.

He compared his situation to Trump’s two impeachments and acquittals during his first term, saying that the president had “come back stronger”.

Trump, for his part, has said that he would stand by Hegseth even if he is impeached, calling Massie a “stone-cold loser”.

Is impeachment likely to succeed?

Republicans control the House until January 3, when Democrats take over. If most Democrats follow their House leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who says he is a “hard yes”, Massie would only need a handful of Republicans to support the resolution.

Conviction is another story. Even if the House chooses to impeach, Republicans currently hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats, and Democrats, expected to have about 54 next year, would still fall far short of the 67 supermajority of votes needed to oust Hegseth from office.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, expected to become Senate majority leader once the new Congress is seated, has said that Hegseth “must stand trial before the Senate”.

Massie, meanwhile, has urged Trump to act first.

“President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate,” he said.

articles.title: Israeli settlers torch machinery in attack on Palestinian industrial zone
articles.summary: Israeli settlers torch machinery in attack on Palestinian industrial zone Submitted by Muhammad Ateeq on Tue, 11/10/2026 - 13:58 The assault destroys machinery worth more than $1m and threatens the livelihoods of hundreds of Palestinian workers and their families Settlers torched excavators, vehicles and pieces of equipment belonging to local stone-cutting workshops in Beita, near Nablus, in the occupied West Bank, 10 November 2026 (Muhammad Ateeq/MEE) Off Israeli settlers attacked an industrial zone in the Palestinian town of Beita, south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, on Monday, setting fire to heavy machinery, vehicles and equipment and causing extensive damage. Dozens of settlers stormed the industrial zone and torched three excavators, along with several other vehicles and pieces of equipment belonging to local stone-cutting workshops. Ashraf Ghazaly, the owner of the heavy machinery, said more than 150 settlers took part in the attack. They threw stones at Palestinian workers before storming one of the workshops and setting fire to machinery, vehicles and equipment. Ghazaly estimated the losses at more than 3.3 million shekels (approximately $1m). One excavator had been purchased just four days earlier. "They assaulted my brother and other workers; no one was able to stand up to them or stop them," Ghazaly told Middle East Eye. The settlers came from the "Navitar" settlement, established on land belonging to Beita. This latest attack is part of a series of repeated settler assaults on Beita’s industrial zone, which houses stone-cutting workshops, other businesses and heavy machinery that provide a vital source of income for dozens of families and workers in the town. According to Ghazaly, two previous attacks in recent months involved settlers smashing the windows of bulldozers, excavators and offices. A campaign of intimidation Ziad Ghazaly, one of the owners of a family-run industrial facility in Beita, said that settlers used ladders to enter the quarry yard, which lies about 2.5 to three metres below ground level, before setting fire to machinery and facilities within minutes. He said the fire was extensive, despite residents' efforts to help the owners and extinguish the blaze. "The Israeli army arrived at the scene and prevented anyone from entering or leaving, which hindered attempts to bring the fire under control and assist the facility owners," he told MEE. 'The goal of these attacks is clear: to terrorise the owners and workers, forcing them to leave' - Abdul Rahman Salameh, workshop owener Abdul Rahman Salameh, who owns a stone-cutting workshop in the town, said the attack took place after most workers and business owners had left for the day. Only seven or eight young men remained, including his sons and cousins. He said settlers targeted several industrial facilities, setting fire to machinery and equipment. Around five facilities were affected, causing significant material damage. "The area is subjected to frequent provocations and threats from settlers, occurring two or three times a week. The goal of these attacks is clear: to terrorise the owners and workers, forcing them to leave so that the settlers can seize more land and expand," he said. Salameh said they remained determined to stay despite the continued assaults. He added that settlers were seeking to impose a new reality through violence and intimidation, even in Area B of the West Bank, which falls under Palestinian Authority administrative control. Livelihoods at risk The industrial zone in Beita is a vital hub for the construction industry in the northern West Bank, supporting the livelihoods of numerous families, merchants and industrial workers. Omar Diriya, chairman of the board of the Union of Stone and Marble Industry in Palestine, said the attacks target more than industrial facilities and equipment: they threaten the livelihoods of hundreds of Palestinian families. He said the zone’s facilities employ more than 500 workers, supporting hundreds of households, each with an average of six to eight members. Diriya described the repeated attacks on quarries and industrial facilities across the West Bank, including the burning of equipment, as a dangerous escalation targeting the Palestinian industrial sector. The machinery destroyed by settlers is worth more than $1m (Muhammad Ateeq/MEE) He warned that continued attacks threaten not only the property of factory owners and workers but also their lives. "The industrial sector is already grappling with difficult economic conditions exacerbated by closures, checkpoints, bypass roads and high production costs, as well as the difficulties of exporting Palestinian products and restricted access to markets," he said. The destruction of machinery further compounds the losses for facility owners, particularly as insurance companies typically do not cover damage resulting from war or conflict, he added. Diriya also criticised the lack of adequate government plans to support industrial facilities, compensate those affected and strengthen their resilience. The attack on the industrial zone in Beita comes amid an unprecedented escalation in settler attacks in the West Bank. The United Nations humanitarian affairs office (Ocha) documented 397 attacks resulting in injuries or property damage between 1 and 26 October. This was the highest monthly figure since the agency began keeping records in 2006. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, an official Palestinian government agency monitoring settler violence, recorded 1,369 settler attacks overall during October, an increase of more than 111 percent compared with September. articles.body:
World News

Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington renews its push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion nearly five years ago.

The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions.

Hopes of progress in ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks early this year. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Olga was jolted awake by an explosion so powerful that her apartment building shuddered and the windows and furniture shook. Looking outside, she saw a plume of thick black smoke rising from a military equipment factory that had just been hit by a missile.

Residents panicked, said Olga, a 49-year-old choreographer. “We didn’t know whether we should run to a shelter,” she said. The strike on the plant left six people dead and another 26 injured, according to the local governor.

Olga doesn’t live in Kyiv, Kherson or any other Ukrainian city that’s been pounded for years by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces. This is Kirov, a Russian city about 800 kilometers northeast of Moscow known for its 16th century onion-domed monastery rather than being in a war zone.

articles.title: Gli Stati Uniti sbilanciano le trattative tra russi e ucraini
articles.summary: I rappresentati dei due paesi in guerra sono ad Abu Dhabi per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Ma l’accondiscendenza di Trump verso Putin non fa ben sperare
articles.preview: Il 10 novembre russi e ucraini si ritrovano faccia a faccia ad Abu Dhabi, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Insieme a loro ci sono Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, gli inviati di Donald Trump. Gli europei sono stati consultati, ma resteranno comunque esclusi dal dialogo. Ancora una volta emerge il solito interrogativo: è possibile fermare questa guerra che dura da quasi cinque anni e ha provocato un’ecatombe?
articles.body:
Il 10 novembre russi e ucraini si ritrovano faccia a faccia ad Abu Dhabi, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Insieme a loro ci sono Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, gli inviati di Donald Trump. Gli europei sono stati consultati, ma resteranno comunque esclusi dal dialogo.

Ancora una volta emerge il solito interrogativo: è possibile fermare questa guerra che dura da quasi cinque anni e ha provocato un’ecatombe? Secondo i dati dell’istituto di statistica russo, rubati e diffusi da un gruppo di hacker, i morti sul fronte russo sarebbero 400mila, mentre le ultime stime parlano di 100mila vittime ucraine. Per non dire delle sofferenze di un popolo intero, che si appresta a trascorrere l’inverno più duro dall’inizio del conflitto.

Gli unici a volere un accordo a tutti i costi sono gli inviati di Trump. Il presidente statunitense, infatti, ha subìto una sconfitta elettorale umiliante e ha bisogno di cancellare l’immagine di loser, perdente. Il problema è che Trump appare del tutto accondiscendente nei confronti del presidente russo Vladimir Putin, come dimostra il fatto che alla vigilia dell’incontro abbia continuato ad attaccare quello ucraino, Volodymyr Zelenskyj, accusandolo di “mancanza di rispetto” nei confronti della Russia, senza criticare minimamente i bombardamenti dell’esercito russo contro obiettivi civili.

Tutto questo non lascia certo presagire una soluzione rapida, tanto più che Putin sembra convinto di poter piegare durante l’inverno la resistenza ucraina, approfittando delle difficoltà della difesa aerea del nemico e dei danni inflitti alle infrastrutture civili. Quasi ogni giorno la Russia compie azioni che costituirebbero crimini di guerra se solo il diritto internazionale umanitario fosse minimamente rispettato. Putin, però, può contare sulla debolezza degli europei e sulla certezza che Trump chiuderà un occhio.

Il presidente russo è sicuramente entusiasta davanti allo spettacolo delle divisioni europee, a cominciare dai sondaggi francesi che indicano come favoriti per il secondo turno due candidati che, ognuno a modo suo, indebolirebbero il sostegno all’Ucraina. Marine Le Pen ha dichiarato che la Francia “non ha più i mezzi” per assistere Kiev, mentre Jean-Luc Mélenchon propone un referendum nelle zone del Donbass controllate dall’esercito russo.

Il 9 novembre Kiev ha risposto al candidato della France insoumise ricordando il referendum del 1991 con cui l’83 per cento degli abitanti del Donbass votò per l’indipendenza, aggiungendo che “i referendum sotto occupazione sono uno strumento di annessione, non un’espressione della volontà popolare. Nessun paese civile e democratico accetterebbe questo processo per stabilire i suoi confini”.

L’Ucraina può sperare che la presenza degli europei ad Abu Dhabi, anche se nell’anticamera degli incontri e non al tavolo dei negoziati, possa scongiurare un tradimento troppo clamoroso. Di recente i rappresentanti del continente sono rimasti sconvolti quando hanno scoperto (all’ultimo minuto) che Trump aveva deciso di cancellare le sanzioni contro la Russia nel tentativo, poi risultato inutile, di far abbassare il prezzo del petrolio e limitare le perdite alle elezioni di metà mandato.

Per gli ucraini il nuovo parlamento statunitense, che si insedierà all’inizio di gennaio, è una buona notizia, perché vigilerà sull’applicazione delle sanzioni adottate in primavera su iniziativa del senatore repubblicano Lindsey Graham, morto poco dopo. Di sicuro il nuovo congresso sarà meno incline a favorire Putin.

Intanto il teatro pseudodiplomatico si sposta ad Abu Dhabi. Tuttavia, il tentativo di relegare la guerra in Ucraina all’ombra di un’altra guerra, quella in Iran, che Trump non riesce a risolvere, non lascia molto spazio all’ottimismo.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.body:
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced a measure to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, roughly one week after the unpopular Iran war the Pentagon chief championed fueled a midterm defeat for President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

Massie launched his new bid to oust Hegseth as the House of Representatives resumed work following the midterm elections. He posted his resolution outlining charges against Trump’s defense secretary on social media earlier in the day, and introducing the measure on Monday sets up a floor vote on the motion as soon as Wednesday.

“The reality is, we’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran,” Massie told reporters Monday. “He was very effective at extrajudicial killings. There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective. The argument here is that he’s broken laws, and he’s violated the Constitution. And so, that’s the question put in front of my colleagues.”

articles.body:
Antalya, Turkey – Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall slightly in 2026 due to the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock sparked by the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday.

Emissions from the burning of oil, gas and coal — the main drivers of climate change — rose by 0.9% per year, on average, in the past decade, hitting a record high in 2025, according to the Global Carbon Budget report.

But they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026, according to the research, published as nations meet at the U.N.’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

It would be the first annual drop since 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic paralyzed the global economy, trade and transport.

This year, the U.S.-led war in Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz played a role in driving emissions down as it caused a drop in oil consumption amid soaring crude prices, the researchers found.

The deployment of solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles also contributed to the drop. Two thirds of the increase in global energy demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, the report found.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter in Britain.

“The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies,” said Friedlingstein, who led the study published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

Corinne Le Quere, a climate change science professor at the University of East Anglia, noted that emissions rebounded when economies recovered following shocks such as COVID-19 or the global financial crisis.

A rebound is likely “when the oil tensions go away,“ she said in a media briefing.

Oil-related emissions are projected to drop 1.9% last year, but it was “likely a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict,“ the researchers said.

Gas emissions are set to fall 0.3% while those from coal use will rise 0.6%.

Overall, fossil carbon dioxide emissions are expected to reach 38.2 billion metric tons in 2026.

Including emissions from land-use change such as deforestation, total CO2 emissions are projected to rise to 43.3 billion metric tons, from 42.8 billion metric tons last year.

The researchers said land-use emissions are projected to rise partly due to peat fires and forest degradation in southeast Asia, associated with drier conditions linked to this year’s exceptionally strong El Nino climate pattern.

The report found that the world’s carbon budget — the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming exceeds 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels — stands at 150 billion metric tons.

The researchers calculated that at the current, the carbon budget would be exhausted in less than four years.

Nations agreed at the 2015 U.N. climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2C above preindustrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C.

But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.

Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

articles.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
articles.preview: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise. articles.body:
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter â around Â£460 extra a year for the typical UK household â according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard â and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

Two decisions

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.

Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra Â£63bn â around Â£2,200 each â according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.

But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."

There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

The case for drilling

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"

Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".

"If we use our own gasâ¦ that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.

Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.

But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year â even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.

With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.

The case for electrons

The alternative is to build.

Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ãrsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.

Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.

All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.

The China question

And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.

And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.

I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".

Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.

Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.

"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.

Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.

Foreign investment, then - just not from China.

Role reversal

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says â a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest â and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.

And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.

If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices â and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

articles.body:
Ukraine, Russia and US return to talks in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?

November 10, 2026

Ukrainian and Russian representatives last met in February for talks on ending the war, but the same sticking points remain. Ukraine continues to demand security guarantees, which is a non-starter for Russia.

A new round of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere.

When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.

Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.

"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."

Who is sitting at the table?

Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.

The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.

The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.

Europe joins in

Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.

These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.

It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal.

Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."

She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.

"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.

"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."

However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.

She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.

This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.

But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.

Oleshky truce as a template for wider ceasefire?

Late last week, Trump spoke of a "big beautiful agreement," after speaking with Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, "that might involve all of Europe."

This new security architecture, Kushner later clarified on social media, would be centered around "permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability."

These points "don't contain anything the Russians haven't been talking about since 2009," Shelest said.

Ivan Us, chief consultant and economic diplomacy expert at Ukraine's National Institute for Strategic Studies, pointed out that negotiations with people who are not decisions-makers could be simply for show.

But he agreed with other expert observers that negotiators in Abu Dhabi might try to use the temporary truce brokered for Oleshky as a model for other limited humanitarian ceasefires in the region.

But while Us said he saw cause for optimism, he also cautioned that Russia had continued attacks in Ukraine during the Oleshky truce and had used the pause to fortify its positions around the town.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.body:
Kenya

Kenyan police have confiscated 454 kilograms of methamphetamine valued at $27 million in a joint operation with Tanzanian authorities targeting cross-border drug trafficking.

The drugs were discovered in Msambweni, on Kenya's coast, following investigations that began with the arrest of a suspect in Tanzania last week.

According to police, the suspect was transferred to Kenya and helped investigators locate the consignment. The individual was also allegedly connected to an earlier seizure of 250 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine and cocaine in Tanzania.

Three other suspects, including two Tanzanians and a Ugandan, were arrested during the operation. All four remain in police custody pending court appearances.

Officers also confiscated two vehicles and a motorcycle believed to be linked to the operation.

The seizure comes amid growing concern over drug trafficking along East Africa's coastline.

Last month, Kenyan authorities destroyed more than a tonne of methamphetamine intercepted by the country's navy off the coast of Mombasa last year.

Kenya's Deputy President Kithure Kindiki has identified illegal drugs and alcohol abuse as major national threats, pledging tougher legislation and increased enforcement.

The Institute for Security Studies has warned that East Africa is increasingly becoming both a transit corridor for international drug shipments and a destination for illicit substances.

Police say investigations into the latest seizure are continuing.
