articles.body:
Some Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors published a statement yesterday saying they would not vote for games that use generative AI in “any capacity.” Soon after, the developer of indie hit Big Walk has published a statement saying it “sparingly” used AI in the “final stretch” of the game’s development to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.”

Big Walk’s developers said that they used AI ‘sparingly’ to help work through ‘difficult technical challenges.’

According to the jurors’ statement, while this year’s IGF entries have been “incredible,” there has been “a significant increase” in the number of games “developed with generative AI tools,” leading to “fairly intense discussion and disagreement” with no “universal consensus.” The statement includes a list of beliefs, including that generative AI has “negative effects,” that AI-generated code is “not an exception to these harms,” and that use of AI tools is “not a forgone conclusion in our industry.”

IGF jurors that signed include Telling Lies and Immortality creator Sam Barlow and Celeste composer Lena Raine. The jurors say that the statement doesn’t speak for IGF as an organization or for all IGF jury members, noting that some voiced concern about being able to safely sign “without professional blowback.”

One contentious title was apparently Big Walk, the co-op adventure game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House. In a statement to Aftermath and posted on its website, House House said that “In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.”

House House said its “primary use case” of LLMs was “to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code,” including fixing an issue with shadows by modifying LLM-suggested code. House House noted it turned to the “LLM chatbot” after researching the problem “extensively” and even speaking to an engineer at Unity.

The studio said it disclosed its AI usage as part of its IGF submission, though it has not disclosed AI usage on Big Walk’s Steam page because “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.”

“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House said. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable’. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”

House House didn’t have an AI policy in place when it developed Big Walk, which it described as a “failure,” and said it will “work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.”

Earlier this year, Claude Code went through its own particular hype cycle. And now, Anthropic is trying to expand its footprint
articles.body:
For years, Anthropic has been known for its focus on enterprise and coding tools that attract high-flying corporate clients, inspiring competing frontier labs — like OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and Meta — to copy its strategies. Earlier this year, Claude Code went through its own particular hype cycle. And now, Anthropic is trying to expand its footprint to other knowledge workers with an AI-powered suite of office tools.

The company is courting white-collar workers ahead of its IPO.

At an event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Anthropic unveiled new tools for non-technical workers who spend a lot of time attending meetings, brainstorming new ideas, and analyzing metrics: Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards. The tools allow for Claude to join a meeting, take notes, lay out ideas on a shared whiteboard, edit spreadsheets alongside employees, or turn a presentation into a one-minute explainer video. The new “Artifacts,” or Anthropic’s version of graphical UI, come two and a half years after Artifacts first debuted, and join existing tools like Claude Docs, Slides, Design and Motion.

Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Meetings are all now available in beta, with the first two available to all paid plans and Meetings available for Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The company also announced that Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards when it was introduced in beta in October) is now generally available to all paid plans.

Nicholas Lin, who works on product at Anthropic, told The Verge in a pre-briefing that Claude Code “changed how engineers work a year ago” — and now, the company is looking to knowledge workers as “the gap we’re hoping to close.”

“I think there’s still a lot of friction when it comes to adopting AI for non-developers,” he said.

The company also unveiled new interactive connectors that allow for users to open apps from partnered companies, such as HubSpot, Adobe, and Atlassian, inside Claude. The company launched Model Context Protocol about two years ago, and its marketplace of tools has grown to more than 9,000 plugin options; now, Lin says, the company is looking to make those connections a lot deeper, so that users don’t have to switch tabs to access the services they use every day and instead just embed them into Claude. For example, with the new tools, people can access a native Adobe PDF editor or a HubSpot marketing campaign tracker inside Claude itself.

The tools follow other AI companies’ offerings in recent years: Google’s Gemini can join meetings and take live notes, and so can OpenAI’s ChatGPT, in some cases, via its “record” feature. Gemini is also well-versed in creating spreadsheets (thanks to Google Sheets), and Google has a lot of different “interactive connectors” for its suite of office tools. At OpenAI’s DevDay last month, OpenAI leaned even further into integrated apps and connectors in order to make its new Dots agents more useful. Anthropic is following in some of their footsteps, plus trying to gain new ground in the AI agent race.

The company is under a lot of pressure to generate more revenue and drive more product engagement ahead of its IPO, as it’s slated to potentially make the most valuable public debut of all time. And although that will turn heads, it also translates to a lot of pressure from investors, who want to see a viable path to profit at Anthropic.

The tools Anthropic debuted on Tuesday are some of the company’s first native products for non-technical knowledge workers. Lin said that although Claude Cowork, one of the company’s other tools for non-engineers, is essentially a wrapper for Claude Code, that tool was aimed at the “technical parts of [Anthropic’s] non-technical audience,” Lin said.

“Now we want to expand that reach toward everybody else.”

articles.title: Anthropic launches Claude Meetings to turn workplace discussions into plans and tasks

The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets. articles.body:
Anthropic announced new workplace features on Tuesday, including Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls to begin working on tasks while participants are still talking. The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets.

The launch of Anthropic’s new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google. Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks.

With Claude Meetings, teams can add Claude to a video call as a visible participant. Claude then follows the conversation and gets to work on tasks in real time. As participants talk, it can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year’s figures. After the call, the meeting notes, action items, and other materials Claude created are available in claude.ai.

The work that comes out of a meeting usually starts after everyone hangs up, but with this new feature, teams can turn discussions into actions in real time, Anthropic says.

Claude identifies itself as a meeting participant and posts a notice in the meeting chat. It won’t join calls with external guests unless authorized by an admin, and will automatically leave if an external guest joins.

Claude Meetings is launching in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. At launch, it works with Google Meet, with support for additional plans expected to follow.

As for Claude Whiteboards, Anthropic describes the feature as a collaborative board where teams can talk through a plan and have Claude turn it into an organized visual workspace with timelines and deadlines.

The company notes that many people already brainstorm with Claude, but that in order to share their results with others, they would have to copy-paste them somewhere else. Now, a team can work directly with Claude on the same board in real time.

When the brainstorm is done, Claude can turn the board into a doc or a slide deck. Additionally, Whiteboards also work inside Claude Meetings, so the board builds while people talk, Anthropic says.

Claude Whiteboards is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop, and mobile.

The company also launched Claude Sheets, which lets teams create and collaboratively edit spreadsheets with Claude. A team can ask it to build a campaign tracker or hiring budget, and Claude will then generate a working spreadsheet.

Anthropic says Claude handles the initial setup of trackers and budgets, while allowing teams to continue refining and updating the same spreadsheet. Each spreadsheet can include multiple tabs, formulas, formatting, and dropdown menus. Claude also makes edits directly in cells alongside the team, and outlines each change so users can see what it did.

Claude Sheets is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop and mobile.

Anthropic also announced that Claude Data, formerly known as Claude Dashboards, is now generally available. The feature connects Claude to systems that companies use to keep their numbers, like a data warehouse or CRM. Users can ask questions, and Claude responds with dashboards, written data stories, or narrated videos.

Additionally, the company announced interactive connectors that open the full version of apps like Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot inside Claude. Anthropic notes that teams can now open these apps directly alongside their Claude conversations and ask the assistant to work within them, essentially bringing existing workflows into the same workspace.

articles.title: Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion valuation in massive stock market debut
articles.summary: The maker of Claude is looking to raise up to $64.4bn in one of the largest IPOs in history next week.

articles.body:
The maker of Claude is looking to raise up to $64.4bn in one of the largest IPOs in history next week.

Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion for its upcoming IPO, with the company looking to raise as much as $64.4bn in what would be one of the largest stock market debuts in history.

The company, which makes the Claude AI chatbot, launched its investor roadshow on Tuesday, with reported plans to go public next week.

According to its filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Tuesday, Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78, giving it a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion when potential shares are included.

It has also secured $26bn in a separate private placement backed by some of the world’s largest tech companies, including Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and AMD.

The listing is being closely watched as a major test for how much investors are still willing to bet on AI companies, which have driven huge gains in tech stocks and the broader US market.

The $1.4 trillion valuation is lower than earlier estimates, which had suggested Anthropic could be valued between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, as concerns grow about the company’s enormous infrastructure spending and recent swings in AI stock prices.

Those concerns extend beyond Anthropic, with investors increasingly questioning whether AI companies can make enough money to justify their soaring valuations and sustain the boom.

Despite the uncertainty, Anthropic’s growth has been explosive.

The company reported revenues of $17bn in their third quarter, up from $1.4bn a year earlier, as its net losses narrowed. On Tuesday, Anthropic said it was on pace to generate about $81bn in annual revenue, $10bn higher than its estimate a month earlier.

The company credits its growth to the demand for Claude, including from industries like healthcare, financial services and legal services.

But to keep up with that demand, Anthropic has committed almost $900bn to computing costs with partners including Amazon and Google, a massive financial bet on continued demand for its product.

The IPO also lands in an uncertain political climate, with Democrats having just won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections last week. The new Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate have raised the prospect of more regulation of AI companies and new restrictions on the construction of data centres that power the technology.

AI stocks slid after the midterms, with the Nasdaq falling 5.5 percent on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop in more than a year. The selloff, also driven by declines at Nvidia, whose CEO was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy, wiped out trillions of dollars from the market.

Markets have since recovered some of those losses, though the Nasdaq dipped slightly below 1 percent on Tuesday. Some analysts argued the sell-off was an overreaction and that the election was unlikely to derail the expansion of data centres.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy: a timeline
articles.summary: The affair could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
articles.preview: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing.
articles.body:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.

United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements (November 9, 2026)

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy (November 9 -10, 2026)

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became a Nvidia preferred cloud partner giving it priority access to chips, the Information reported. The Info reported that Shanghai Century Litong. facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 US government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.

Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person” (November 8, 2026)

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia Board of Directors begins investigation (November 8, 2026)

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing (November 5, 2026)

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy (October 29, 2026)

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

A Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy (Spring 2026)

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers which warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO, but does not take action (Late 2025)

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship to Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.

The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.

U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations (October 2025)

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.

Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, a Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

articles.body:
Google is rolling out its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, to the general public after releasing it to a select group of “cybersecurity defenders” two weeks ago. Google claims Carbon is its “strongest model” yet, and capable of competing with the very best systems from Anthropic and OpenAI.

It ‘pushes the frontier even further’ than its last release, Argon.

Google says Gemini 4 Carbon “pushes the frontier even further” than Argon, referring to the company’s other frontier model that launched only last month. The company said Argon will likely remain “the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work,” but that Carbon is “built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence,” such as complex, multi-step coding and open-ended scientific research.

To highlight Carbon’s utility for long-horizon work involving AI agents, Google said it is also previewing a “swarm” feature on its agentic development platform Antigravity, which will let users turn a single prompt “into a coordinated team of agents.”

Carbon is rolling out today via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, Google said in a blog post. It will also be available to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, the AI Mode in Search, and on Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Carbon will be available to lower tier subscribers or free users.

As with the launch of Argon, Google is pricing Carbon very competitively. The model is launching with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and a quarter the cost of Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model, which launched yesterday. Even after those costs double at the end November — when the introductory period of lower prices finishes — Carbon will still be significantly cheaper than frontier rivals on a per-token basis, though this doesn’t necessarily translate to lower costs as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks.

Benchmarks cited by Google when it first announced Carbon suggest the model is one of the most powerful on the market across most metrics, behind Fable 5.2. It should be noted that companies can and do cherry-pick benchmark results to show their tools in the best possible light.

The release, hot on the heels of Argon, marks a decisive return for Google at the very forefront of AI research. For months, frontier development looked like a two-horse race between Anthropic and OpenAI.

articles.title: Iran denies role in fridge hack, France summons ambassador
articles.summary: France has said it rules "nothing" out in response to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration units. Iran, however, said it categorically rejected Paris' "baseless and one-sided accusations" of IRGC involvement.
articles.preview: Iran denies role in French fridge cyberattack as Paris summons envoy November 10, 2026 France has said it rules "nothing" out in response to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration units. Iran, however, said it categorically rejected Paris' "baseless and one-sided accusations" of IRGC involvement. Iran on Tuesday dismissed French accusations that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets last month, as Paris summoned Tehran's ambassador to discuss the incident.
articles.body:
Iran denies role in French fridge cyberattack as Paris summons envoy

November 10, 2026

France has said it rules "nothing" out in response to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration units. Iran, however, said it categorically rejected Paris' "baseless and one-sided accusations" of IRGC involvement.

Iran on Tuesday dismissed French accusations that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets last month, as Paris summoned Tehran's ambassador to discuss the incident.

"Iran's Foreign Ministry categorically rejects the French government's baseless and one-sided accusations against Iran regarding alleged cyber activities in France," the ministry said, adding that it "strongly condemns this hackneyed policy of leveling accusations against the Islamic Republic."

The alleged attack, which began overnight on October 11-12, raised the temperatures in supermarket refrigerators and freezer units, spoiling produce and even causing fires in isolated instances.

A series of similar incidents have since followed in Europe and beyond, even including a failed attack on cooling units at French blood banks this month, though it is not yet clear if these subsequent events are connected.

France summons ambassador, says it rules 'nothing' out in response

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday that his government would "rule nothing out and will take all measures — including those we may not disclose publicly — that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks."

Barrot was speaking amid a G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris that included discussions with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the conflict with Iran.

Barrot even said that despite a change in tone from the Trump administration since the midterm election defeat in the US, the risk of a renewed escalation with Iran could not be ruled out, "otherwise, we would not have devoted so much time and energy over the past two days to addressing these issues with our American counterpart."

France summoned the Iranian ambassador on Tuesday and said it would be seeking European-level sanctions in response.

The EU said it would seek to provide a "swift and united response" pending discussion with member states.

"As the EU, we have consistently called on all states to refrain from malicious behavior in the cyberspace, and we will continue to address such malicious behavior, making use of all the tools that we have, also under the EU cyber diplomacy toolbox, including sanctions," spokesman Anouar El Anouni said.

Barrot said that the goal of any response would be "to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again."

Iran accuses French of 'projecting' its own failures

Tehran appeared to threaten retaliatory measures of its own if sanctions materialized, saying it would "not hesitate to take necessary and appropriate measures to safeguard its national interests and security in the face of unlawful foreign activities."

It accused France of "merely projecting its own governance failures" with its allegations.

"A government that cannot even manage the temperature of its own refrigerators now seeks to shift the blame onto foreign actors through these preposterous accusations," it said.

What did Paris prosecutors say about suspected Iranian involvement?

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday that she had opened an investigation into leading members of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit that is part of Iran's multi-force specialist military, the IRGC, that answers directly to its religious leadership.

She said her office had requested arrest warrants against two Shahid Kaveh officials and was investigating others.

She described the entity as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps."

French cyber intelligence agencies said the unit conducted "large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for the purpose of sabotage." It said it primarily targeted Israel and the US, but also France and other European countries.

Beccuau said that the attack targeted roughly 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets. It used web interfaces to "initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles," and also to disable automated alerts from sensors designed to go off when temperatures exceeded certain levels.

Sweden's Civil Defense Minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin warned that more cyberattacks could be expected in the coming months, as AI tools make it easier to detect and exploit vulnerabilities.

He said that it was not yet possible to say if hacks targeted Swedish supermarkets last week were connected, not least because the type of sabotage would have "been easy to copy" after seeing the initial reports in October.

articles.title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips
articles.summary: Google's new tensor processing units (TPUs) broaden its chip portfolio to more use cases: confidential model training and more memory capacity.
articles.preview: Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house-developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads.
articles.body:
Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house-developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads.

The new units, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, are part of the company’s eighth generation of chips introduced in April this year, and build on what those chips offered, which was more inference capacity and support for large training requirements.

TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t chip, and is geared specifically for confidentially training and running AI models, Google said in a blog post. The chip “builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use,” the company wrote.

The chip also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training, so it can be used to distill and train small models on the fly. That ability, according to Google, could prove useful for cases where a company might want to train a model on its proprietary data without having to move the data between devices.

Meanwhile, TPU 8i Max basically combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips the company launched in April, doubling the memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, but in a single package. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries.

The chip launch comes as hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, and even AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are working on their own lines of AI-specific semiconductors and accompanying software in order to reduce their reliance on the dominance of Nvidia.

The news also comes at a particularly vulnerable moment for Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend admitted to having an affair with someone alleged to be a Chinese spy.

articles.title: What is Shahid Kaveh, ⁠⁠the Iran cyberunit tied to France’s fridge hacking?
articles.summary: IRGC-linked unit operates through front groups posing as vigilante hackers to hit adversaries, says French intelligence.
articles.preview: What is Shahid Kaveh, the Iran cyberunit tied to France’s fridge hacking? IRGC-linked unit operates through front groups posing as vigilante hackers to hit adversaries, says French intelligence. The French government has accused Shahid Kaveh – a group it says is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) – of being behind recent cyberattacks targeting refrigerators in French supermarkets.
articles.body:
What is Shahid Kaveh, the Iran cyberunit tied to France’s fridge hacking?

IRGC-linked unit operates through front groups posing as vigilante hackers to hit adversaries, says French intelligence.

The French government has accused Shahid Kaveh – a group it says is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) – of being behind recent cyberattacks targeting refrigerators in French supermarkets.

The alleged sabotage campaign last month hacked into refrigeration systems in hundreds of stores in France and remotely cranked up temperatures, spoiling millions of euros’ worth of food.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has called the attack “unprecedented in its level of aggression”.

But in a statement on Tuesday, Iran denied any role in the cyberattacks.

Here’s what we know about Shahid Kevah and its alleged involvement:

What has France accused Iran of?

French officials have accused the IRGC of orchestrating the October 11-12 cyberattack, which they say targeted 700 commercial sites across France.

In a statement, the Paris prosecutor’s office specifically blamed Shahid Kaveh, which it described as a “an offensive cyberunit” affiliated with the IRGC’s cyberelectronic command (CEC).

A report published by France’s spy and cyberagencies also named three alleged perpetrators – Hamid Reza Lashgarian, who it described as the head of the CEC, and Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand, who it identified as commanders in the Shahid Kaveh unit.

How has Iran responded?

Iran pushed back against the accusations on Tuesday, calling them “baseless and biased”.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry, in a statement, described the accusations as a “highly irresponsible and contemptible action to tarnish Iran’s image and disrupt its relations with other countries”.

The statement warned that Tehran would not hesitate to take measures to safeguard its national interests and security.

It made no mention of the Shahid Kaveh unit.

What is Shahid Kaveh?

Iran’s government has never publicly acknowledged the existence or purpose of the group, which appears to be named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an IRGC commander who died aged 25 in 1986 during the Iran-Iraq war.

But Western intelligence agencies have linked it to the IRGC, assessing that it is part of a network of hackers operating under Tehran’s direction.

In their recent report, French spy and cyber agencies said Shahid Kaveh operates through numerous front groups posing as vigilante hackers, including “CyberAveng3rs” and “Cyber Isnaad Front.”

Those front groups, it said, “are tasked with publicly claiming responsibility for certain attacks carried out by the Shahid Kaveh unit”.

Two of the alleged associates named by French intelligence agencies – Hamid Reza Lashgarian and Mahdi Lashgarian – have previously been sanctioned by the US over alleged ties to the IRGC’s cyberunit.

What do we know about Iran’s cyberattack capabilities?

Iran has extensive cybercapabilities that it is increasingly using to advance its wartime objectives, say experts.

Nikita Shah, a senior fellow with the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology programme at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), says there has been a “notable uptick in Iran’s cyberoperations since March 2026”, including “cyberespionage” and “conflict-themed cybercrime”.

“Iran’s cyberoperators will likely be working on preparing new technical accesses, and possibly new cyber capabilities to leverage, should the conflict continue over the longer term or negotiations falter,” Shah wrote in an August analysis for CSIS.

A 2025 policy report by the United Kingdom Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee describes Iran as “an aggressive cyberactor with extensive capabilities”.

While Iran’s cybercapacity is not as sophisticated as Russia’s or China’s, according to the report, Tehran is adept at using basic exploitation methods against its adversaries.

“Whilst Iranian cyberactors often use simple computer network exploitation techniques, they use them very effectively, exploiting basic vulnerabilities that many organisations have, including in the UK,” said the report.

Cyberoperations are also a “deniable tool” that Iran can use to “attack its enemies, respond to perceived aggression and project power in the region – and globally,” the report added.

Other than France, who else has been targeted?

The IRGC and affiliated groups have been linked to past cyberattacks on targets in the United States and Israel, including water infrastructure.

One wave of attacks in late 2023 targeted US water facilities that relied on a computer system made by Israeli software firm Unitronics, according to US cybersecurity officials.

Earlier this year, Iran-affiliated hackers also went after industrial control technology used in US infrastructure, including at government facilities, US security agencies warned. The hackers were able to disrupt some programmable logic controllers (PLCs) — technology that helps automate and monitor machinery and manufacturing processes — across several US critical infrastructure sectors, causing “operational disruption and financial loss”, the US agencies said.

And in March this year, an Iran-linked hacking group claimed to carry out a destructive cyberattack on US-based medical device provider, Stryker.

The recent French intelligence report said attacks by Shahid Kaveh and its affiliated groups have been “primarily directed against Israel and the United States, but also against France and other European countries”.

articles.body:
Un ripasso dei primati dell'azienda, per capire quella che potrebbe essere la storia di spionaggio industriale più clamorosa degli ultimi tempi

Lo scorso luglio la polizia di Singapore ha sequestrato una villa del valore di circa 42 milioni di dollari che sarebbe stata comprata con i soldi del contrabbando di merci verso la Cina. A essere contrabbandati non erano né armi né stupefacenti ma dei chip sviluppati dall’azienda statunitense Nvidia, e in particolare quelli per lo sviluppo di sistemi di intelligenza artificiale (AI), così avanzati che il governo statunitense ne ha vietato l’esportazione in Cina.

Che la Cina faccia di tutto per avere accesso ai chip di Nvidia è noto da tempo: secondo l’intelligence statunitense, però, non si limita al contrabbando. La relazione intima ammessa nei giorni scorsi dal CEO Jensen Huang con l’imprenditrice cinese Alice Huang potrebbe essere uno dei più gravi casi di spionaggio industriale nel settore tecnologico.

Per capire cosa voglia la Cina da Nvidia serve partire da cosa renda questa azienda così importante. Nvidia ha il monopolio di fatto nella progettazione di GPU, chip progettati per eseguire moltissimi calcoli in parallelo, di cui detiene l’84 per cento del mercato. Inizialmente, le GPU servivano ad avere una resa grafica migliore; il calcolo parallelo si è rivelato poi utile anche in altri ambiti, tra cui negli ultimi anni lo sviluppo dei sistemi di intelligenza artificiale. Proprio la corsa agli investimenti nel settore delle AI ha causato la crescita senza precedenti registrata dall’azienda negli ultimi anni, che oggi è la seconda società al mondo per capitalizzazione di mercato dopo Apple.

Nvidia non produce le sue GPU, si limita a progettarle: la produzione vera e propria è affidata a TSMC, azienda con sede a Taiwan leader globale nella produzione dei chip più potenti. Nvidia è insomma un business “fabless”, cioè senza un impianto di produzione.

Delegare la produzione a un’azienda esterna ha permesso a Nvidia di specializzarsi su altri aspetti dello sviluppo tecnologico. Il suo dominio si basa infatti anche su CUDA, un’architettura software e hardware con cui gli sviluppatori possono adattare il funzionamento dei chip alle proprie esigenze. Lanciata nel 2007, CUDA ha oggi più di sette milioni di utenti, è soprattutto un software pensato per il settore delle AI ed è uno dei principali punti di forza di Nvidia, visto che si può usare solo con le sue GPU. Qualunque azienda volesse replicare il modello dell’azienda, infatti, dovrebbe sviluppare una piattaforma paragonabile a CUDA, oltre che progettare chip tra i più avanzati al mondo.

Oggi praticamente tutte le aziende del settore AI usano (almeno in parte) GPU Nvidia per lo sviluppo e il funzionamento dei loro modelli. Anche per questo, negli ultimi anni sono aumentati gli investimenti per creare chip alternativi, per rispondere all’enorme domanda da parte del settore delle AI: Google, ad esempio, ha sviluppato internamente le TPU, chip progettati espressamente per lo sviluppo di queste tecnologie.

Sono soprattutto le aziende cinesi, però, a soffrire la mancanza d’accesso diretto alle GPU di Nvidia: secondo alcune inchieste giornalistiche, aziende di AI cinesi come DeepSeek avrebbero ottenuto illegalmente dei chip Nvidia. Al tempo stesso, il governo cinese sta investendo molto sulle aziende locali affinché sviluppino delle GPU paragonabili a quelle di Nvidia. La più attiva su questo fronte è Huawei, ma lo stesso stanno facendo anche aziende come Alibaba e Cambricon.

La Cina sta quindi cercando di replicare in casa i progressi tecnologici di Nvidia, obiettivo a cui lo spionaggio di Alice Huang potrebbe aver dato un contributo importante. Pur non essendo la prima volta che in un’azienda tecnologica statunitense si infiltra una spia cinese questo è senz’altro il caso più ambizioso e rilevante, soprattutto per via del peso che Nvidia ha in tutto il settore. Anche TSMC subisce da tempo spionaggio industriale da parte cinese: per esempio quest’estate Taiwan ha accusato un ex dipendente di TSMC di aver copiato segreti industriali per fornirli alla Cina.

Secondo l’intelligence statunitense, Alice Huang sarebbe stata reclutata dal governo cinese per ottenere informazioni su Nvidia e sui suoi fornitori, ma anche su Jensen Huang stesso, che in questi anni è diventato una delle persone più ascoltate dal presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump in tutto il settore tecnologico. Anche grazie a questo rapporto personale, negli ultimi due anni Trump ha mantenuto una politica molto favorevole nei confronti delle AI e dei data center (business che dipende in buona parte dalle GPU di Nvidia). Lo scorso dicembre Trump permise all’azienda di tornare a vendere un suo chip piuttosto potente nel mercato cinese: una decisione che all’epoca fu criticata anche all’interno del partito Repubblicano.

articles.body:
OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over the Medicare data breach, but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.

Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.

A key recommendation is for the Attorney-General’s Department, the Australian federal police and home affairs to consider introducing “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence, which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.

The rapid review came in response to an AI agent, developed by OpenAI, accessing data from Services Australia and three other systems in June. The company did not notify the Australian government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August, prompting criticism from Labor and Albanese.

Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies:

- Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.

- Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.

- Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.

- Allowing independent evaluation of their models.

- Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.

- Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting”, including around AI agents behaving in ways their creators may not have intended.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, appearing with Albanese, told reporters: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.”

“We need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do,” Burke said.

“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately.”

Despite the government’s earlier public anger at OpenAI, Albanese on Tuesday characterised the company’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy. Guardian Australia understands OpenAI is unlikely to face further legal proceedings related to the June breach.

While Albanese did not directly answer a question about whether the OpenAI incident in June would have breached the proposed new laws if they were in place, government sources indicated that the new legislation would address similar future incidents.

“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details,” Albanese said.

“All of that was confirmed essentially … but that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”

In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was reviewing the recommendations and the government’s proposals.

“We have been in close dialogue with the government and we’ll continue to engage constructively as it develops its proposed legislation,” they said.

A separate OpenAI-led process, which is discussing better coordination between AI developers and the government, is expected to report back by 31 December.

The rapid review made 18 recommendations. Albanese said “we accept all of the recommendations and we’ve commenced work to implement them”.

The AI researcher Toby Walsh said the people in charge of AI companies needed to be criminally liable.

“We’ve tried fining them and we’re not the only ones. These companies are incredibly wealthy and it’s almost impossible to fine them enough,” Walsh said.

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, branded Tuesday’s announcement a “capitulation” to the AI industry, claiming the reforms would not do enough to change behaviour. He said the government should have committed to implementing stronger changes rather than the recommendation to “consider” them.

“Safety keeps coming second to corporate investment, and this review locks that priority in by tying every AI safety effort to bringing in more AI money and more datacentres,” Shoebridge claimed.

“Being a world leader in AI doesn’t mean being a doormat to big tech. It means being prepared to regulate it, to protect Australians and to make sure corporate profits don’t come at the expense of everyone else.”

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said the Coalition backed the announcement. He said “AI is too important to become an unnecessarily partisan political contest”, signalling an “enduring and multi-partisan approach” to the technology.

The Digital Agency maintains that the system is secure because data is decentralized and stored across multiple locations, including local governments and businesses. articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.summary: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.
articles.preview: Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack. In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
articles.body:
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.

On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.

AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".

"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.

One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .

This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".

The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.

This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.

In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.

OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.

It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.

Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

articles.title: Quanto conta Jensen Huang per Nvidia
articles.summary: L'uomo al centro del caso di presunto spionaggio cinese è uno dei CEO più longevi e potenti del settore tecnologico
articles.preview: L'uomo al centro del caso di presunto spionaggio cinese è uno dei CEO più longevi e potenti del settore tecnologico Quando un amministratore delegato finisce al centro di un presunto tentativo di spionaggio da parte di una potenza straniera, la sua posizione diventa molto difficile e le pressioni perché lasci l’incarico possono crescere rapidamente. Se poi quel CEO guidasse una delle aziende più strategiche nella competizione tecnologica internazionale, ci si aspetterebbe che anche le più alte cariche politiche del suo paese ne chiedessero le dimissioni.
articles.body:
L'uomo al centro del caso di presunto spionaggio cinese è uno dei CEO più longevi e potenti del settore tecnologico

Quando un amministratore delegato finisce al centro di un presunto tentativo di spionaggio da parte di una potenza straniera, la sua posizione diventa molto difficile e le pressioni perché lasci l’incarico possono crescere rapidamente. Se poi quel CEO guidasse una delle aziende più strategiche nella competizione tecnologica internazionale, ci si aspetterebbe che anche le più alte cariche politiche del suo paese ne chiedessero le dimissioni. E la pressione sarebbe ancora maggiore se fosse anche uno dei consiglieri scelti direttamente dal presidente per orientare la politica del paese sulle tecnologie fondamentali per la sicurezza.

Nel caso di Jensen Huang, il CEO di Nvidia che ha ammesso di aver avuto una relazione con una donna sospettata di essere una spia assoldata dal governo cinese, sta succedendo quasi il contrario.

La donna in questione si chiama Alice Huang e, secondo quanto emerso da informazioni dell’intelligence statunitense riportate dalla stampa, potrebbe essere stata reclutata dalla Cina per raccogliere informazioni su Jensen Huang e su Nvidia. Il consiglio di amministrazione di Nvidia ha aperto un’indagine indipendente per capire se siano stati compromessi segreti aziendali o la sicurezza nazionale, ma allo stesso tempo ha ribadito pubblicamente di avere piena fiducia in lui. Il presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump lo ha definito «una brava persona» e «un uomo onorevole», aggiungendo che probabilmente «ha una spiegazione» per quanto accaduto.

A spiegare tutta questa indulgenza è almeno in parte il ruolo che Huang ha dentro Nvidia, quotata come la seconda società al mondo e che finora nel 2026 ha generato 215,9 miliardi di dollari di ricavi, il 65 per cento in più rispetto all’anno precedente. Le sue GPU, chip progettati per eseguire moltissimi calcoli in parallelo, eseguono gran parte dei calcoli necessari per costruire e addestrare i modelli di intelligenza artificiale. Da loro dipendono aziende come OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Meta e Google.

Huang è uno dei CEO più longevi della Silicon Valley e non ha successori designati: una cosa che già all’inizio del 2026 Bloomberg aveva definito molto insolita per una società di tali dimensioni.

Huang è a capo di Nvidia da più di trent’anni: a lui vengono attribuite molte delle scelte decisive che l’hanno resa così grande ed è sempre lui a rappresentarla davanti a investitori, governi e clienti. Anche il suo modo di gestire l’azienda è diventato parte dell’identità di Nvidia: lui lo riassume provocatoriamente con l’espressione «torture them into greatness», più o meno «tormentali finché non diventano eccellenti»: dice di preferire continuare a mettere sotto pressione una persona perché migliori invece di rinunciarci e licenziarla.

Huang fondò Nvidia nel 1993 per costruire i chip che gestiscono la grafica dei videogiochi nei computer, insieme agli ingegneri Chris Malachowsky, ancora oggi dirigente tecnico dell’azienda, e Curtis Priem, che ne fu direttore tecnologico fino al 2003. Il loro primo prodotto portò Nvidia quasi al fallimento: il chip NV1, infatti, funzionava benissimo, ma elaborava la grafica tridimensionale con un sistema diverso da quello usato da Microsoft, che sarebbe poi diventato lo standard per la maggior parte degli sviluppatori.

Huang decise di cambiare approccio, licenziò metà dei dipendenti di Nvidia e scommise tutto su RIVA 128, un processore che non era nemmeno stato testato. Quando arrivò sul mercato, Nvidia aveva ormai denaro rimasto per circa un mese di stipendi. Ne vendette un milione di unità in quattro mesi: RIVA 128 offriva infatti in un’unica scheda grafica sia il 2D necessario per usare normalmente il computer, sia il 3D dei videogiochi, convincendo molti produttori di computer a installarlo direttamente nelle loro macchine.

Da quel momento, raccontano i suoi dipendenti, Huang ha cominciato a comportarsi come se il fallimento potesse essere sempre dietro l’angolo, una cosa che ha ricordato per anni nei suoi discorsi ai dipendenti.

In effetti i momenti difficili per Nvidia non erano finiti. Nel 2006 presentò CUDA, una piattaforma che permetteva di usare le GPU, che erano state sviluppate per la grafica dei videogiochi, anche per le simulazioni scientifiche e l’analisi di grandi quantità di dati. Huang decise di rendere tutte le sue GPU compatibili con CUDA, aumentando il costo dei chip al punto da assorbire i profitti lordi dell’azienda. Alla fine del 2008 il titolo Nvidia aveva perso circa il 70 per cento del suo valore.

Poi nel 2012 tre ricercatori mostrarono che quando una rete neurale, cioè il tipo di sistema alla base della maggior parte dell’intelligenza artificiale moderna, veniva addestrata utilizzando le GPU di Nvidia poteva ottenere risultati eccezionali nel riconoscimento delle immagini. Huang decise così di investire tutto nell’intelligenza artificiale: un dirigente dell’azienda, Greg Estes, ha raccontato che Huang comunicò la decisione con una mail inviata un venerdì sera e che il lunedì Nvidia si comportava già come un’azienda di AI.

Huang fece una scommessa simile anche con i data center quando nel 2019 decise di investire 6,9 miliardi di dollari per Mellanox, un’azienda specializzata nelle tecnologie che permettono a migliaia di processori di comunicare ad altissima velocità. Era la tecnologia che poi sarebbe stata alla base del funzionamento delle IA, che richiedono migliaia o decine di migliaia di GPU collegate tra loro.

Tutto questo è stato possibile anche per il modo in cui Huang gestisce l’azienda: ci sono circa sessanta dirigenti e Huang ha incontri diretti con tutti loro. Organizza le riunioni in modo che le discussioni avvengano davanti a più persone contemporaneamente, per far sì che tutti possano ascoltare quale sia il problema, il ragionamento con cui viene affrontato e il percorso che porta alla soluzione. Anche gli errori vengono trattati allo stesso modo: Huang chiede ai suoi dipendenti di presentare davanti a centinaia di persone la catena di decisioni che hanno portato a un errore, in modo che tutti possano evitare di ripeterla.

Huang ha anche reso Nvidia un’azienda di famiglia, una cosa insolita nella Silicon Valley. Ci lavorano il figlio Spencer Huang, la figlia Madison Huang e il genero. La moglie Lori Huang, invece, presiede la Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, un ente che finanzia università, ricerca e progetti filantropici. La vicenda, che ha fatto emergere le vulnerabilità della sicurezza aziendale, rischia di avere ripercussioni anche sugli equilibri interni e sulla gestione di Nvidia, coinvolgendo direttamente una famiglia diventata negli ultimi anni sempre più presente e visibile nell’azienda. Huang aveva persino detto, quando i figli erano più giovani, che il suo sogno sarebbe stato vedere un giorno uno di loro guidare Nvidia.

Quando in un’intervista venne detto a Huang che i suoi collaboratori lo descrivevano come «esigente», «perfezionista» e una persona «non facile per cui lavorare», lui rispose che la descrizione era perfettamente corretta e che fare cose straordinarie non è facile.

articles.body:
I dati dell’Osservatorio Jfc: prezzi in aumento, spesa media per una famiglia in settimana bianca di 4.101 euro. Nel ranking delle destinazioni vince Cortina d’Ampezzo

La voglia di neve non passa ma inflazione e potere d’acquisto indebolito rendono la settimana bianca un sogno non sempre realizzabile per le famiglie italiane: nell’inverno 2026-2027 il fatturato complessivo della montagna arriverà a 12,86 miliardi di euro (+5,2%) rispetto all’anno precedente ma a salvare la stagione saranno gli sciatori stranieri. È quanto emerge dalla nuova edizione dell’Osservatorio italiano del turismo montano di Jfc: le previsioni parlano di flussi internazionali in crescita (+5,7%), mentre il mercato nazionale arretra (-3,4%). Intanto nel ranking delle destinazioni messo a punto dalla società di ricerca guidata Massimo Ferruzzi al primo posto si conferma Cortina d’Ampezzo, mentre Bormio scala quattro posizioni i si piazza al terzo posto.

Il fatturato in crescita

A spingere il fatturato della stagione saranno le strutture ricettive alberghiere ed extra-alberghiere con 6,392 miliardi (+7,4%), seguite dai servizi (noleggio attrezzature, maestri di sci, skipass) a 4,987 miliardi (+3,3%) e ristorazione e commercio, 1,457 miliardi (2,6%). Il fatturato complessivo del sistema salirà a quota 12,8 miliardi, segnando nei confronti della stagione 2025 /2026 una crescita di oltre 636 milioni di euro sul dato a consuntivo, con una variazione complessiva positiva del 5,2%.

I prezzi in aumento

Trascorrere un soggiorno invernale sulla neve costerà in media il 5,6% in più rispetto allo scorso inverno. I prezzi delle scuole di sci cresceranno del 3,4%, gli impianti di risalita del 4,6%. Ma i valori più sono quelli di bar e ristoranti (+7,9%) e alberghi (+6,6% anche se per le settimane bianche l’incrmento è solo dello 0,8%).

La spesa: 4.101 euro per una settimana bianca in famiglia

Quanto spenderanno gli italiani per un soggiorno in montagna il prossimo inverno? Secondo le rilevazioni Jfc 1.573 euro a persona adulta per trascorrere una settimana bianca in Italia; spesa che sale a 4.101 per un nucleo familiare composto dai genitori e da un figlio di età inferiore agli 8 anni.

Per trascorrere un fine settimana sulla neve in Italia la spesa media a persona adulta è di 669 euro che arriva a 1.899 per un nucleo familiareI

E con la flessione dei redditi mancano i presupposti per favorire gli investimenti in macchine e tecnologie per l’agricoltura.
articles.body:
FederUnacoma: l’aumento dei costi produttivi impatta anche sul mercato dei trattori. calo del 5,4% in Italia e del 13% negli Usa. La presidente Maschio: le vendite ripartiranno

L’esplosione dei costi produttivi sta provocando una profonda erosione dei redditi agricoli. E con la flessione dei redditi mancano i presupposti per favorire gli investimenti in macchine e tecnologie per l’agricoltura. È con questo complesso scenario congiunturale che si apre oggi a Bologna l’edizione 2026 di Eima, il salone delle macchine e delle tecnologie per l’agricoltura organizzato da FederUnacoma (l’associazione dei costruttori italiani).

Forte calo dei redditi in Europa e Usa

«I produttori agricoli – ha spiegato la presidente di FederUnacoma, Mariateresa Maschio ricevono una quota molto limitata del prezzo che i consumatori pagano. Negli Stati Uniti, le aziende ricevono meno di 12 centesimi di ogni dollaro di cibo prodotto, quota che cala a 6,7 cent al netto dei costi. In Europa i produttori ottengono circa un quarto del valore aggiunto della filiera agroalimentare. Una quota che rischia di ridursi ancora a causa dell’incremento dei costi».

E con i redditi frenano anche gli investimenti

Difficoltà che si riversano sul mercato dei macchinari. I dati aggiornati ad ottobre - elaborati da FederUnacoma sulla base delle immatricolazioni fornite dal Ministero dei Trasporti - indicano un calo del 5,4% per le trattrici, del 9% per i trasponder, del 7,3% per i rimorchi. Restano in positivo solo le mietitrebbiatrici (+10,4% a fronte di 245 macchine vendute).

Cala il mercato nazionale ma anche quello internazionale. Negli Stati Uniti, tra gennaio e settembre le trattrici hanno perso il 13%. In Canada le vendite hanno registrato un -9%. Peggio ancora in America Latina con la flessione del 19% in Brasile e del -27% in Argentina. Meno accentuate ma sempre in negativo le vendite in Europa il -6% della Germania, il -3,3% della Francia, il -4,6% della Spagna e il -18,8% della Polonia.

Un ridimensionamento del mercato che spinge alla frenata la produzione nazionale che, secondo le stime di FederUnacoma, dovrebbe vedere nel 2026 un calo in valore della produzione di trattrici del 4,7% (a quota 1,8 miliardi di euro).

articles.body:
EU seeks to pick new ECB head by year end: Eurogroup chief said

November 9, 2026

Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of December.

The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, announced on October 29 that she is stepping down from the position prematurely, nine months before the end of her term.

Lagarde's decision to step down early makes the schedule tight for EU leaders because they must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board within months.

"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.

"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.

Who are the candidates?

The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International Settlements, Pablo Hernandez de Cos from Spain.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.

The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.

Dutch minister says the choice needs to be 'merit based'

Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position," referring to his long-standing experience.

"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfill this position."

Heinen also said countries should not see the ECB leadership contest as one between northern and southern European countries, or as an "opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.

A package deal is expected

The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, whose term ends in May 2027.

The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the main eurozone countries — France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.

The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.

"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.

Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.

"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."
